title: Highlighting Success of Problem-Solving Courts, Chief Judge Seeks Funding to Expand Programs
author: JEREMY SODERGREN
description: The state court system will be putting a heavy emphasis on more specialized courts this coming year, including drug treatment courts, veteran courts and alternative-to-incarceration courts. Chief…
content:
Legislative Gazette photo by Quintin Fisher
Chief Judge Rowan Wilson spoke in the chamber of the New York State Court of Appeals to call for the legislature to include funding for the state's problem-solving courts in this session's budget. The state court system will be putting a heavy emphasis on more specialized courts this coming year, including drug treatment courts, veteran courts and alternative-to-incarceration courts. Chief Judge Rowan Wilson outlined his goals for the court system in his State of the Judiciary address last month. He used the word, unorthodox, to explain his vision for the year and the address held on Feb. 27. Rather than explaining these goals himself, Chief Judge Wilson hosted a number of speakers who talked about their life-changing experiences within the state's court system, with an emphasis on the ways alternatives to traditional courts have helped them and their constituents. Wilson called on the Legislature to increase funding for those problem-solving courts that offer solutions for troubled families, those dealing with addiction and military veterans who could use a second chance, instead of facing jail time. One of the speakers, Keisha Nankoosingh, spoke about her time with the Monroe County Judicial Diversion program with the Felony Drug Court. Nankoosingh was introduced by Kimberly VanCamp, the project director of the Seventh Judicial District Treatment Court. VanCamp began by speaking about the requirements a participant must meet to be a part of the diversion program. 'Successful completion of substance use disorder treatment, sustained abstinence from mood altering chemicals,' she said. 'They must have a high school diploma [or equivalent], complete community service hours, be gainfully employed and have no new arrests. Sounds simple right?' Despite the long list of necessary requirements Nankoosingh was able to meet, keep and exceed those requirements through to the completion of the program and is now a certified recovery peer advocate. 'Ten years ago, my life was very different. For over a decade [my partner and I were] dependent on drugs and alcohol. There were times during active use that we wanted to change and get sober but couldn't stay committed,' she said. 'In the end we had no money, no job, no transportation, no home and we pushed our friends and families away. Then all of the ‘not-yets' started to happen that resulted in some criminal charges.' At Nankoosingh's arraignment she was facing up to seven years in prison, but was told she may qualify for treatment court, one of the specialized courts designed to not incarcerate individuals who can qualify for their different programs. 'I was relieved because I knew that I needed help and I knew that the treatment courts could provide me with the tools I'd need to sustain my sobriety,' she said. 'I was told that successful completion of the program would result in no criminal convictions. Choosing treatment court was the best decision of my life, and my partner also chose treatment court.' Nankoosingh's journey did not come without loss however. Her partner did not complete the treatment court program and was sentenced. Shortly after his release from prison, he became ill and passed away in 2020, she said. 'These are the stakes. It's life or death,' Nankoosingh said. 'Treatment court gave me the support and hope that I needed to live.' Legislative Gazette photo by Quintin Fisher
Governor Kathy Hochul spoke at the State of the Judiciary reaffirming her support of Chief Judge Wilson and the state's court system. Chief Judge Wilson had a number of other speakers come in and talk about their experiences with these specialized courts. From veterans courts to family courts, people shared their struggles and how these alternatives to the traditional court system have benefitted them and worked to keep them on straight paths. 'Due to past fiscal crises and a company of budget cuts, the courts have been forced to make do with less,' Chief Judge Wilson said in his closing remarks. 'With greater resources, not just for the courts themselves, but for the attorneys and ancillary providers vital to treating troubled New Yorkers with professionalism, care and compassion, I am confident that we can find ourselves overflowing with happy endings.'

title: Governor Signs Law Requiring Suicide Hotline Info on College ID Cards
author: JANANI HARIRAM
description: Gov. Kathy Hochul signed the Student Lifeline Act and announced a statewide campaign to raise suicide prevention awareness among college students and other at-risk groups. The Student Lifeline Act, or…
content:
Photos by Darren McGee, courtesy of the Governor's Office
September 9, 2024 — Rochester, NY — Gov. Kathy Hochul signs the Student Lifeline Act, sponsored by Assemblywoman Sarah Clark, left and Sen. Samra Brouk, right, while announcing a new multimedia campaign to promote mental health.
Gov. Kathy Hochul signed the Student Lifeline Act and announced a statewide campaign to raise suicide prevention awareness among college students and other at-risk groups.
The Student Lifeline Act, or legislation S.1865-B / A.6563-A , requires an education campaign about the federal 988 suicide and crisis lifeline, ordering both to be printed on college student identification cards.
The 988 number provides a 24/7 connection to trained counselors who can help anyone thinking about suicide, struggling with substance use, experiencing a mental health crisis, or any other kind of emotional distress
The bill's sponsor memo states, 'Suicide is the second leading cause of death for college students in the United States… Providing students with information on available resources, including contact information on identification cards, ensures that students are aware of these resources and are able to access them quickly and easily.'
The bill was sponsored by Senator Samra Brouk, chair of the Committee on Mental Health, and Assemblywoman Sarah Clark, a member of the Higher Education Committee.
Brouk said, 'Mental health and stress are affecting college students on a profound level — this Student Lifeline bill is lifesaving legislation that can prevent crises for students and their families.'
The Student Lifeline Act also requires all New York colleges to provide resources to students explaining in what circumstances the 988 number should be used. Any colleges that do not issue ID cards will still need to distribute 988 information through other means annually.
In conjunction with Suicide Prevention Month, New York State's Office of Mental Health (OMH) is launching a $5 million public awareness campaign. Using the slogan 'We Hear You,' the campaign aims to encourage residents to use the 988 helpline if they or someone they know is going through a mental health crisis.
The campaign is specifically aimed at those demographics who could benefit from the helpline but had the lowest recognition of this service in focus groups. These groups include first-responders, school and college aged students, and Black, Latina and/or LGBTQ+ individuals.
According to the OMH , 'While the suicide rate in New York State has remained relatively stable since 2012, a recent report by the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention highlighted racial/ethnic disparities, including among black and Hispanic individuals.'
There is a strong connection between substance abuse and suicide rates. Last year, the State began a five-year $10 million effort, funded through the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services' Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, to address behavioral problems with youths around the state.
By boosting funding for 988 from $35 million to $60 million per year, starting the 'We Hear You' awareness campaign, reconvening the Suicide Prevention Task Force, and funding other initiatives to help prevent youth suicide rates, Hochul shows that she is passionate about this issue.
Hochul said, 'As we recognize Suicide Prevention Month, we must ensure all New Yorkers are aware of this critical resource [988] and are willing to use it whenever they or someone they know needs help.'

title: AOC Joins Congressman Ryan at SUNY New Paltz, Tells Students: You Can Decide Who Controls The House
author: PATRICK KELLY
description: NEW PALTZ, N.Y. — Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Rep. Pat Ryan held a joint "Get Out The Vote" rally on the campus of SUNY New Paltz last week, reminding students they are at 'ground zero' for some…
content:
Photo courtesy of Pat Ryan for Congress, via Facebook
NEW PALTZ, N.Y. — Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Rep. Pat Ryan held a joint 'Get Out The Vote' rally on the campus of SUNY New Paltz last week, reminding students they are at 'ground zero' for some of the most hotly contested races in Congress this election year.
The event, a rally to engage young voters, featured speeches from both representatives urging New Paltz students to vote in the upcoming election, paying special attention to the congressional races.
The event, sponsored by The New Paltz College Democrats, was by reservation only and quickly sold out. The auditorium, which seats 280, was at capacity when the event started.
The Pro-Palestine group 'No Votes for Genocide' protested outside, urging students to vote blank as an alternative to voting for candidates who have been supportive of Israel's war in Gaza. Protestors surrounded Coykendall Science Hall, the building where the rally took place, and as participants of the rally exited, protesters banged on the doors to the building, which saw an increased security presence throughout the afternoon.
Ryan spoke first, emphasizing the importance of the election and participating in the campaigns of local Democrats. Ryan, formerly the Ulster County executive and long-time resident of the county, highlighted his connection to the area, joking with the crowd that he and his wife Rebecca 'had several SUNY New Paltz students that have babysat for [them].'
'We are sitting in the Hudson Valley in New Paltz in literal ground zero for where the direction of this country is going,' Ryan said, later claiming that some politicians 'have lost their way, and forgotten their values.'
'If you're willing, you have an opportunity, and I would argue, an obligation, to do whatever you can in this moment,' Ryan said. 'If you all walk out of here and are willing to be part of our campaign in voting and talking to other students on this campus and on other campuses, you literally are the margin of victory to make sure we can hold our seat.'
Ryan then criticized the current Speaker of the House, Mike Jonhson, saying 'he was the legal architect of the entire election denial effort' by former President Donald Trump, contrasting him with Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, and would-be speaker if Democrats win a majority in the upcoming election.
'The other opportunity we have is to elect a New Yorker and somebody who is the antithesis of that [Mike Johnson] in many, many ways,' Ryan said. 'Hakeem Jeffries, who would make history as the first Black speaker of the House in our country's history. Too long in the making.'
Ryan then introduced Ocasio-Cortez, who entered to a standing ovation from the crowd. Ocasio-Cortez, who urged the participants to call her by her moniker AOC, expressed her excitement by saying 'I'm really thrilled to be here because of this moment in time that we are in, and when I think about this moment in time that we are in, it's such a moment of massive transition.'
Ocasio-Cortez emphasized the power of the youth vote in 2024. Photo courtesy of the New Paltz College Democrats
'So many of us have inherited nonsense. We were born into so much inherited injustice, and so many of us in our generation have not gotten a fair shake,' said the congresswoman, adding that she 'was elected by young people.'
'The only reason I won is because voter turnout increased by 68 percent and the number of voters under 45 matched or outpaced the number of voters over 60,' she said.
Ocasio-Cortez also 'bragged' on behalf of Ryan, highlighting his commitment to constituents and saying that he 'not bought' and hasn't taken any corporate PAC money.
At this point, protestors, who attended the event, interrupted the speech by shouting that Representative Ryan took money from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), which has proved controversial in this election cycle for funding opponents of progressive House members, like Rep. Cori Bush and Rep. Jamaal Bowman, who along with Ocasio-Cortez, are considered members of the 'Squad.'
Ryan has received $5,000 in PAC money and $169,764 in individual donations from AIPAC, making for $174,764 in total , according to campaign finance transparency organization OpenSecrets.
Ocasio-Cortez acknowledged the protest, saying 'We're in an extremely painful time. So I want to make space for that.' She pivoted to say that Ryan 'stood up' to large corporations like 'GE that were dumping chemicals right here in the Hudson [River] for little kids to consume.'
'You know how hard it is to stand up to one of the largest corporations in the world and say, not here? He does that. We cannot take that for granted.'
Winding down her speech, Ocasio-Cortez said that despite its appearance as a safe blue state, Democrats in New York cannot take anything for granted, considering what is at stake on November 5.
'The actual balance of this country runs through New York. We're a swing state y'all. We may not be a swing state on the presidential level…we should not take any of that for granted. What folks may not think of this as a swing state on a presidential or a statewide level, but the entire balance of the U.S. House of Representatives runs through Ulster County, Long Island, Westchester, upstate and Buffalo.'
Ocasio-Cortez stressed the point repeatedly that in the upcoming election, 'Our state can determine who is in the majority.'
In closing, Ocasio-Cortez rallied the audience again, saying that New Paltz could make a difference in the election. 'New Paltz is going to elect a House Democratic majority. New Paltz is going ot make sure that we send those resources after we elect Pat Ryan, and that we continue to support a Senate majority and Democratic White House, because the only way we're going to do this is through sustained trifecta, baby, and thats what we're coming for.'

title: Alison Esposito Concedes, Pat Ryan Holds On To Hudson Valley Congressional Seat
author: JANANI HARIRAM
description: NEW PALTZ— On November 5, incumbent Pat Ryan won the congressional race for New York's 18th District with nearly 57 percent of the vote, beating Republican challenger Alison Esposito. Esposito…
content:
Photo courtesy of Patrick Ryan for Ulster County, via Facebook
NEW PALTZ— On November 5, incumbent Pat Ryan won the congressional race for New York's 18th District with nearly 57 percent of the vote, beating Republican challenger Alison Esposito.
Esposito conceded on the same day, writing in her statement, 'I would like to congratulate Congressman Pat Ryan on his relection and wish him and his family all the best moving forward. I want to extend a heartfelt thank you to my supporters, hard-working volunteers, and staff. Thank you for your countless hours of dedication and support throughout this race.'
Esposito, a retired deputy inspector with the New York City Police Department, won 43.4 percent of the vote, with more than 95 percent of election districts reporting.
'I will never stop fighting to bring common sense back to our government,' she said. 'I hope that Congressman Ryan will fight for the issues that thousands of NY-18 residents who voted for me care so deeply about. My commitment to New Yorkers remains unwavering.'
In his acceptance speech Ryan said, 'I respect her [Esposito] and I respect the fact that she called me and conceded this race.'
The district, comprised of Orange and parts of Dutchess and Ulster counties, has been represented by a Democrat in Congress since 1983.
The 18th District seat was a hotly contested race, with the debates between Ryan and Esposito covering issues such as abortion, gun control, and housing costs, with Ryan focusing heavily on preserving reproductive freedom and abortion rights.
Ryan said, 'We centered this campaign on freedom. On patriotism. On an optimistic forward-looking vision for our country. We really did our best to bring people together and call to the best in people.'

title: After NY Doctor's Indictment, Gov. Signs Law That Protects the Identity of Abortion Pill Prescribers
author: OLIVIA SHULTS
description: On Monday, Gov. Kathy Hochul confirmed New York's status as a safe haven for reproductive health care, following the indictment of New York Dr. Margaret Carpenter by a Louisiana grand jury for…
content:
Photo by Mike Groll, courtesy of the Governor's Office
February 3, 2025 – Albany, NY – Gov. Kathy Hochul is joined by lawmakers to sign a new law that will give doctors the option of leaving their names off prescriptions for abortion medicine, listing only the medical practice if they choose. The bill signing came just days after New York Dr. Margaret Carpenter was indicted by a Louisiana grand jury for prescribing an abortion pill online to a minor.
On Monday, Gov. Kathy Hochul confirmed New York's status as a safe haven for reproductive health care, following the indictment of New York Dr. Margaret Carpenter by a Louisiana grand jury for prescribing an abortion pill online to a minor in the southern state.
Joined by dozens of female lawmakers, Gov. Hochul signed the bill S.36-a / A.2145-a , permitting prescription labels for mifepristone, misoprostol, and their generic alternatives to include the name of the prescribing health care practice, rather than the name of the prescriber, at the prescriber's request.
This bill provides additional protection for doctors based in New York, building on the shield law enacted in 2023, designed to provide extensive protection of New York State doctors providing services via telehealth to those in restricted states.
Hochul stated 'We're also requiring that notice be given to the patient that alternative labeling will be used. Other states, they want to target, harass, scare, intimidate doctors and patients. Now that may be okay in a place like Louisiana, maybe Indiana, but those are not our values here in the State of New York. No.'
Alongside Gov. Hochul, bill sponsors Senator Shelley Mayer and Assemblymember Karines Reyes stated their commitment to reproductive rights while discussing the 'urgency and priority this issue takes for us as legislators, New Yorkers, and women,' according to Mayer.
While speaking at the bill signing, Reyes said 'We are committed unequivocally to our state,' demonstrating the willingness of the state legislators to fight for and protect reproductive rights.
Medication abortion has become a primary resource for those seeking abortions across the nation. They account for 63 percent of non-hospital abortions in the United States, as of 2023, not including abortions within total ban states or mail-in medication.
Following the Supreme Court's decision to overturn the constitutional right to an abortion in Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization in June 2022, 17 states have taken steps to limit access to abortion services. Thirteen states imposed a total ban, while another four states prohibit abortions after six weeks, a time when pregnancy is difficult to detect for many individuals. More than half of women between the ages of eighteen and forty-nine live in states with abortion restrictions.
Sen. Michelle Hinchey said 'The fears that many of us had, have now become a reality,' in relation to reproductive healthcare and the changing dynamics within the United States.
Hochul pledged to protect doctors in New York that provide health care to patients out-of-state through this bill. Regarding Dr. Margaret Carpenter, the governor said 'This doctor simply responded to a cry for help, and in return now faces a felony charge that subjects an individual to a prison term of up to five years, and fines as high as $50,000. Think about that. Five years in prison simply because you upheld your oath and delivered medical care.'
She went on to discuss her plan to neglect the request to extradite the doctor to face criminal charges, saying 'Never, under any circumstances, will I sign an extradition agreement that sends our doctor into harm's way to be prosecuted as a criminal for simply following her oath.'
The indictment of Dr. Carpenter is the first case in the U.S. of criminal charges against a doctor accused of prescribing abortion pills to an out-of-state patient since the overturning of Roe v. Wade in 2022. Furthermore, the indictment has the potential to be the first direct test of New York's shield laws, which are expected to protect prescribers who use telehealth to provide medication abortion to patients in states where abortions are banned.
Gov. Hochul stated in regard to New York-based doctors, 'We must be there to support them. We must be their allies. We must be their army to protect them.'
Reyes agreed.
'In New York we say we believe in science, we believe in facts, we trust our clinical providers, and we will protect them every step of the way.'

title: New York Farm Bureau, Gov. Hochul Share Concerns Over Tariff Threats
author: JAMIE CASE
description: The threat of stiff tariffs being imposed on the United States' three biggest agricultural markets has alarmed the New York Farm Bureau and Gov. Kathy Hochul over potential harm to New York's farmers.…
content:
Legislative Gazette file photo
The threat of stiff tariffs being imposed on the United States' three biggest agricultural markets has alarmed the New York Farm Bureau and Gov. Kathy Hochul over potential harm to New York's farmers.
A declaration of an economic emergency called by President Donald Trump would impose duties of 25 percent on imports from Mexico and Canada, with limited exceptions, as well as 10 percent on all imports from China.
Canada and Mexico both announced they would impose retaliatory measures, while making some concessions to appease Trump, leading to a last-minute pause on tariffs with those countries, for now. Trump has yet to reach an agreement with China meaning a U.S. tariff of 10 percent on Chinese imports has already taken effect.
These actual and threatened tariffs have already caused real damage to farmers.
According to American Farm Bureau President Zippy Duvall, over 80 percent of 'potash,' a key fertilizer ingredient, comes from Canada.
Tariffs increasing fertilizer prices could further strain the finances of New York's farm families, already burdened by inflation and rising supply costs. The New York Farm Bureau called upon Congress to take any step necessary to protect farmers from retaliatory tariff measures and create new market opportunities.
According to the New York Farm Bureau, some local farmers are reporting retaliatory measures in Canadian markets, having an impact on their farms; products are reportedly being pulled, or threatened to be pulled, from shelves in Canada upon the announcement of the tariffs.
'While our policy supports fair trade and creating additional markets for our farmers, some of our farmers are reporting that these retaliatory measures are already impacting their farms,' the organization said in a statement on February 3.
According to the Office of the United States Trade Representative, New York exported more than $2 billion in domestic agricultural products in 2022, with the largest exports being dairy products, corn, soybeans and feed grains.
'The strength of our agricultural community in New York comes, in large part, from the diversity of products we grow and produce here,' the Farm Bureau states. 'While we appreciate the one-month delay in implementing tariffs from Canada and Mexico, our concerns still stand.
'We respectfully request that the agricultural community, both in New York and in the greater United States, be top of mind when creating trade policy initiatives. At a time when our farmers continue to operate on razor-thin margins, we ask that Congress take any step necessary to protect them from retaliatory tariff measures, and, instead, create new market opportunities.'
Gov. Kathy Hochul met with Canadian Consul General Tom Clark on February 4 about the possible tariffs affecting New York and Canadian products. Photo by Darren McGee, courtesy of the Governor's Office
February 04, 2025 – Albany, NY – Gov. Kathy Hochul hosts a meeting with Tom Clark, consul general of Canada over the threat of tariffs that would affect their agricultural markets.
'The trade relationship is critical,' Hochul said in a statement following that meeting. 'And the amount of trade; I don't think people can appreciate how that impacts the cost of living in a place like New York. And certainly in Canada, but I have to be laser focused on what's happening to New Yorkers.
'There has been a sense of anxiety now, for a time period, about the cost of everything going up. The cost collectively for a family of four going up to anywhere from $1,300 to $3,000,' Hochul continued. 'I'm working hard to put money back in people's pockets with my budget, and the last thing I want is to have the money taken out of their pockets with higher costs.'
Jamie Case is an undergraduate student at SUNY New Paltz, with expertise in a myriad of media realms. When she's not producing content, she's chopping salads in a college town.

title: Republicans Celebrate as DOT Halts Congestion Pricing; MTA Files Legal Challenge
author: ELIJAH FAZLI
description: The U.S. Department of Transportation announced Wednesday that it will be terminating its approval of New York City's congestion pricing plan, citing concerns about the burden it would have on…
content:
Legislative Gazette file photo
The U.S. Department of Transportation announced Wednesday that it will be terminating its approval of New York City's congestion pricing plan, citing concerns about the burden it would have on taxpayers.
The program went into effect on January, charging drivers a $9 toll for entry into parts of Manhattan south of 60th Street, also known as the congestion relief zone. The purpose of the plan was to effectively reduce pollution, travel time, and traffic by taxing New Yorkers for entering some of the most congested zones, thus creating safer, less crowded streets.
The program was working well, according to data gathered by the MTA during the first week of its implementation.
Estimates showed entries into New York's Central Business District down by 7.51 percent, as well as 30-40 percent shorter travel times on inbound river crossings.
Despite this, Trump-appointed Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy sent a letter to Gov. Kathy Hochul on Wednesday, explaining his decision to eliminate the New York congestion pricing program.
In this letter, Duffy concludes that the Central Business District Tolling Program is not an eligible value pricing pilot program. This is because the program utilizes cordon pricing with no alternate options, meaning drivers are charged regardless of the road they use, with no toll-free option available. Duffy argues that The Federal Highway Authority has never approved a value pricing pilot program of this nature, thus concluding that Congress, in using the vague phrase 'value pricing pilot program' did not actually authorize this pricing method.
Additionally, Duffy said 'Commuters using the highway system to enter New York City have already financed the construction and improvement of these highways through the payment of gas taxes and other taxes. But now the toll program leaves drivers without any free highway alternative, and instead, takes more money from working people to pay for a transit system and not highways. It's backwards and unfair.'
Upon receiving word of the decision, Republican lawmakers and party leaders in New York praised Trump for taking action against the program, such as Republican Chair Ed Cox, who said, 'I commend President Trump for his decisive action in halting Governor Hochul's ill-conceived congestion pricing scheme. This plan was a cash-grab that would have unfairly taxed hardworking New Yorkers, already the most taxed people in the country.'
The president received praise from Assembly Minority Leader Will Barclay, R-Pulaski, as well, who stated 'The Trump Administration's decision to halt congestion pricing is a win for New Yorkers and motorists already burdened by the high cost of living.'
New York Conservative Party Chair Gerard Kassar echoed Duffy's concern about the toll being used primarily as a way to fund the MTA.
'From the start, this tax was a scandal. The hopelessly mismanaged MTA, which fails to collect billions of dollars in fares and tolls each year, again tried to pass the cost of its incompetence onto New Yorkers who are already paying for MTA services,' Kassar said. 'How could Gov. Kathy Hochul and her progressive colleagues not have expected the enormous public blowback?'
Trump himself later posted on his social media platform Truth Social, saying 'CONGESTION PRICING IS DEAD. Manhattan, and all of New York, is SAVED. LONG LIVE THE King!'
While Republicans cite the potential financial burden on New York City commuters as their reason for challenging the program, Trump's social media post points to more than just the will of New Yorkers as motivation to eliminate the program. Many believe he is just doing what he wants, while ignoring laws set in place to regulate his presidential power.
In response to his comment, Hochul stated 'I don't care if you love congestion pricing or hate it. This is an attack on our sovereign identity, our independence from Washington. And we are a nation of states. This is what we fought for. This is what people like Alexander Hamilton and others fought for: To set up a system where we are not subservient to a king or anyone else out of Washington. So this is the fight we're in. It's all about our sovereignty.'
Furthermore, she stated, 'We are a nation of laws, not ruled by a king. The MTA has initiated legal proceedings in the Southern District of New York to preserve this critical program. We'll see you in court.'
The good-government group Reinvent Albany supports the Metropolitan Transit Authority's decision to legally challenge any interference with the congestion pricing program, declaring that 'Under the Constitution of the United States, a president and their executive branch agencies do not have the power to override laws passed by Congress, nor do executive agencies have the power to withdraw federal authorization without a basis in fact.'

title: Facing Tough Questions, DEC Commissioner Touts Clean Water, Land Conservation and Superfund Program
author: MIA QUICK
description: During a sometimes heated budget hearing on environmental conservation and energy, DEC Interim Commissioner Sean Mahar encountered lawmakers with conflicting feelings about the agency's programs and…
content:
Photo courtesy of the New York State Senate
Senator Tom O'Mara, pictured at a budget hearing in Albany on January 28, 2025, said many of New York's climate goals and energy efficiency guidelines aren't realistic under the current timeline and they will lead to higher utility costs for families and businesses.
During a sometimes heated budget hearing on environmental conservation and energy, DEC Interim Commissioner Sean Mahar encountered lawmakers with conflicting feelings about the agency's programs and priorities.
Mahar discussed several DEC accomplishments related to the Community Air Monitoring Initiative, freshwater wetlands, and clean water infrastructure.
The Governor's Office has proposed an All Funds appropriation of $2.6 billion for the DEC, an increase of $83.4 million or 3.3 percent, over the current fiscal year.
The DEC is requesting $627.9 million in State Operations spending, $37.8 million more from last year, to go towards new staff and salary increases and implementing of the Climate Superfund legislation and a program that requires fossil fuel companies to pay into a state fund to help mitigate climate change. The DEC hopes to hire 58 new employees; 30 for the implementation of the Climate Change Superfund Act, eight would be for permitting programs, four to implement the Freshwater Wetlands Act of 2022, four to implement the 30×30 conservation goal and the remainder would be spread among DEC program areas.
The funds will also contribute to thermal energy networks, clean transportation initiatives, and further develop a Cap-and-Invest program. Cap-and-Invest sets a limit on greenhouse gas pollution the state can produce and applies a price to emissions from major greenhouse gas emissions sources. DEC Commissioner Mahar
Mahar emphasized the importance of the Freshwater Wetlands Act in its effort to protect roughly one million acres of wetland habitat and the Community Air Monitoring Initiative, an initiative focused on improving air quality in disadvantaged areas. The $500 million investment by Gov. Kathy Hochul towards clean water infrastructure and its importance received considerable attention from lawmakers, and Mahar.
'The $500 million investment in clean water infrastructure funding is going to continue to leverage and put people to work across the state, bringing on the clean water infrastructure that we need to support our water conservation efforts and management efforts overall,' Mahar said.
Some lawmakers expressed concern over the DEC's ability to complete the '30×30' goal to conserve 30 percent of New York State's land by 2030 and the transition of small businesses away from HFCs and SF6s, two harmful pollutants and potent greenhouse gases, towards more natural, low-emission refrigeration systems.
Sen. Pamela Helming expressed concerns about the potential threat the shift away from HFCS and SF6s may pose to small businesses.
'These businesses are just trying to survive, they don't have time to check DEC's website,' Helming said.
While the majority of senators and Assembly members chose to only ask questions of the DEC administrators, some expressed displeasure at the agency's progress and regulations. Sen. Thomas O'Mara asked for updates on the investigation of the viral Peanut the Squirrel story, Sen. Mario Mattera called battery storage units 'nothing but an experiment,' and Assembly Member Joe Sempolinski voiced his strong objection towards the Climate Change Superfund and the DEC's role in charging companies.
Many of the lawmakers said they plan to meet with Mahar to further discuss individual concerns, the DEC's strategies in detail, and the allocation of funds to specific programs.
Mia Quick is a contributing writer and videographer for The Legislative Gazette, studying Journalism at SUNY New Paltz. She is interested in pursuing environmental and travel journalism during her career.

title: Bill Takes Aim At Deceptive, Misleading Marketing of Unhealthy Food
author: ELIJAH FAZLI
description: Childhood obesity has hit an all-time high as of March 2020, with the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data showing a prevalence of 19.7 percent among U.S. children and adolescents.…
content:
Photo courtesy of the New York State Senate
Childhood obesity has hit an all-time high as of March 2020, with the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data showing a prevalence of 19.7 percent among U.S. children and adolescents.
Citing this data, New York state lawmakers took an important step toward protecting children's health, with the Senate Agricultural Committee passing the Predatory Marketing Prevention Act ( S.397/A.2584 ). The bill was sponsored by State Senator Zellnor Myrie and Assemblymember Karina Reyes and would hold advertisers accountable and limit their ability to promote misleading food marketing.
The legislation would explicitly define and restrict misleading targeted marketing of unhealthy foods and beverages to children and adolescents. The legislation builds on New York's existing false advertising laws, ensuring that young people are not unfairly manipulated into consuming ultra-processed products that negatively impact long-term health.
According to the bill memo, 'the Legislature is morally obligated to protect the public from predatory marketing of junk food consistent with the state's efforts to curb the disastrous health outcomes associated with the overconsumption of these products.'
The bill will now head to the Consumer Protection Committee, where members of the Center for Science in the Public Interest are urging legislators to pass the reform.
Senior Policy Associate Dr. DeAnna Nara said in a statement 'As digital advertising grows more sophisticated, food and beverage companies increasingly rely on data-driven behavioral targeting, influencer promotions, and interactive content to encourage overconsumption of ultra-processed products.'
According to data from the Rudd Center at the University of Connecticut, food, beverage, and restaurant companies spent almost $14 billion on advertising per year, with more than 80 percent of these ads promoting unhealthy foods, such as candy and sugary drinks. In 2021, Sen. Zellnor Myrie dressed as a carrot in Crown Heights, Brooklyn to highlight the importance of his Predatory Marketing Prevention Act. The bill was reintroduced this session and has passed the Senate Agriculture Committee.
Although the amount of food-related advertisements seen by children has declined, these adolescents continue to see more than 1,000 unhealthy food-related advertisements per year, according to research in the Journal of the American Medial Association.
A British study also published by the AMA found that food marketing was significantly associated with increases in food intake and preferences.
These studies point to the greater initiative of food marketing, one that prioritizes getting younger audiences hooked on addictive goods at a young age in order to increase their profit.
Food companies engage in many predatory marketing tactics targeting children. Misleading statements, such as claiming that a product is 'natural' or contains a certain amount of vitamins and nutrients, can mislead audiences into believing that a product is healthier than it actually is.
Marketers will also place celebrities who are typically popular amongst children in their advertising, making the product seem more appealing and thus creating an urge in children to own it.
Data from another UK study published in the journal 'Nutrients' found that the use of celebrities in the marketing of unhealthy food significantly increased consumption of the product.
As advertisers across the United States continue to employ these predatory tactics to take advantage of the minds and desires of adolescents, passage of the Predatory Marketing Prevention act is critical to protecting our youth from manipulating advertising that promotes unhealthy consumption of goods.
'New York has the opportunity to set a national precedent for protecting young people from manipulative advertising that reinforces harmful consumption patterns and undermines efforts to promote lifelong health,' Dr. Nara said.

title: U.S. Department of Education Targeting Three SUNY Schools For Alleged Antisemitic Discrimination
author: THE LEGISLATIVE GAZETTE
description: The U.S. Department of Education on Monday warned three SUNY schools they are under investigation for Title VI violations relating to antisemitic harassment and discrimination. The DOE's Office for…
content:
Legislative Gazette file photo
The U.S. Department of Education on Monday warned three SUNY schools they are under investigation for Title VI violations relating to antisemitic harassment and discrimination.
The DOE's Office for Civil Rights sent letters to 60 colleges and universities — including three SUNY campuses — that they face possible 'enforcement actions' if they do not fulfill their obligations under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act 'to protect Jewish students on campus, including uninterrupted access to campus facilities and educational opportunities.'
'The Department is deeply disappointed that Jewish students studying on elite U.S. campuses continue to fear for their safety amid the relentless antisemitic eruptions that have severely disrupted campus life for more than a year. University leaders must do better,' said Secretary of Education Linda McMahon. 'U.S. colleges and universities benefit from enormous public investments funded by U.S. taxpayers. That support is a privilege and it is contingent on scrupulous adherence to federal antidiscrimination laws.'
SUNY Binghamton, SUNY Purchase and Rockland Community College are the three public colleges identified by the Department of Education as being under investigation.
Five private colleges in New York state — Columbia, Cornell, Sarah Lawrence, Union College and the New School — also received warnings on Monday.
Title VI of the 1964 Civil Rights Act prohibits any institution that receives federal funds from discriminating on the basis of race, color, and national origin. National origin includes Jewish ancestry.
Under President Donald Trump's Executive Order 'Additional Measures to Combat Antisemitism,' the Department has already launched directed investigations into five universities, including Columbia University, where the agency says 'widespread antisemitic harassment' has been reported.
The 55 additional colleges and universities are under investigation, or being monitored, in response to complaints allegedly filed with OCR.
Last week, the Department, alongside fellow members of the Joint Task Force to Combat Antisemitism including the Department of Justice, the Department of Health and Human Services, and the U.S. General Services Administration, announced the cancelation of $400 million in federal grants and contracts to Columbia University.
Last Friday, OCR directed its enforcement staff to make resolving the backlog of complaints alleging antisemitic violence and harassment, many which were allowed to languish unresolved under the previous administration, an immediate priority.
The Legislative Gazette has reached out to the SUNY administration seeking a response.

title: Legislators Join Labor-Religion Coalition to Demand Moral Budget
author: DYLAN MURPHY
description: New York state legislators and members of the Labor Religion Coalition held a rally in the Capitol building's War Room on March 4 to push for investments prioritizing low-income New Yorkers as the…
content: Legislative Gazette photo by Dylan Murphy New York state legislators and members of the Labor Religion Coalition held a rally in the Capitol building's War Room on March 4 to push for investments prioritizing low-income New Yorkers as the Legislature begins to turn their attention to finalizing the budget. Speakers at the event included Assembly members, senators, clergy members and advocates protesting the rising rates of poverty amongst New Yorkers while demanding a 'moral' budget that will hold New York's wealthiest accountable and provide relief to poor and working-class constituents. 'New York has the most income inequality in the country and the highest concentration of extreme wealth. Just 0.4% of the state's population have amassed a combined $6.7 trillion in wealth. Nearly half of that is untaxed investment income,' said Assemblymember Ron Kim, D–Queens, at the press conference. According to a report from the Economic Policy Institute, the top 1% in New York earn more than 40 times those of the bottom 99%. Eight million New Yorkers live in poverty, yet more than 100 billionaires reside in the state. The Labor Religion Coalition warned that Gov. Hochul's prospective budget will only exacerbate the state's inequality, with the budget cutting funds for programs in education, climate infrastructure and Medicaid. 'It is morally indefensible that in a state with such abundance, so many of our fellow New Yorkers struggle to make ends meet,' said Executive Director of the Labor Religion Coalition Reverend West McNeill. Assemblymember Tony Simone, D–Manhattan, offered a personal account of how his district has suffered from widespread poverty and the inequality gap. 'Billionaire's Row sits on one side of the district, with some of the most expensive real estate per square foot in the country, and yet everyday New Yorkers in the same district just a few blocks away are struggling to make ends meet…we must take action to pass a budget this year that prioritizes the working class over the ultra-wealthy in our state.' The advocates also brought attention to New York's tax policy as well, claiming it needs to be more progressive and ensure that the rich are paying their fair share. While a number of millionaires fled New York during the pandemic, a report from The New York Times last year found that they have come back, as lower and working-class families become the demographic leaving the state in droves. 'By championing fair taxation and prioritizing communal well-being over corporate interests, we can pave the way for a brighter tomorrow. Let us heed the call to compassion and solidarity, ensuring that every individual has the opportunity to thrive and flourish in the great state of New York,' said Pastor Brian Ellis-Gibbs of Queens Baptist Church. 'Recent reports show the majority of New Yorkers are in favor of increased taxes on high-income earners and large corporations to improve funding for public programs. It's time to fully fund education, invest in climate justice, and ensure affordable housing for all,' added Assemblymember Harvey Epstein, D–Manhattan. A poll commissioned by Invest in Our New York Campaign and conducted by the Siena College Research Institute found that 74% of New Yorkers believe taxes should go up for the top 5% of earners, and about the same percentage said that taxing the rich should be the solution to a state budget shortfall rather than cutting services. Invest in Our New York Campaign was one of the many groups present at the press conference, and in 2021, they worked with the legislature to increase taxes on millionaires, subsequently creating $10 billion in new, recurring revenue. After the event, advocates delivered a petition with more than 1,000 signatures reiterating their demands to Gov. Hochul.

title: Legislation Would Provide Tax Benefits to Newspapers That Employ Local Journalists
author: DYLAN MURPHY
description: On Feb. 15, more than 100 local newspapers across New York state launched The Empire State News Coalition in an effort to approve a legislative package that several news organizations say would bring…
content: Legislative Gazette file photo On Feb. 15, more than 100 local newspapers across New York state launched The Empire State News Coalition in an effort to approve a legislative package that several news organizations say would bring relief to the struggling local journalism field. The Local Journalism Sustainability Act, S625B / A2958C , would provide tax credits to local news outlets for the employment of local news journalists. Local print and online newspapers with 100 employees or less would receive a 50% tax credit against the first $50,000 of each employee's salary, with a maximum of $200,000 per organization. Just two weeks after the bill was introduced in the Assembly, The Empire State News Coalition launched with newspapers and media organizations from across the state, uniting to advocate for the bill's swift passage through its respective chambers. The bill's Senate sponsor, Brad Hoylman-Sigal, D–Manhattan, said, 'A thriving local news industry is vital to the health of our democracy, and we should do everything in our power to ensure that New Yorkers have access to independent, community-focused journalism. I'm proud that so many publications from every corner of the state have come out in support of this critical legislation.' According to the Hussman School of Journalism and Media at the University of North Carolina, the number of newspapers in New York state have decreased by 40% from 2004 to 2019, with a 63% decrease in circulation. New York's Orleans County became the first in the state to go newspaper-less, and 13 of the state's 62 counties are down to just one newspaper. 'Professionally-reported, fact-checked local news forges community, keeps elected officials in check, and strengthens democracy. This important legislation would help fortify our business and allow us to keep reinvesting in high-quality local journalists,' said Adam Stone, publisher at Examiner Media in Westchester. A study by researchers from St. Olaf College in Northfield, Minnesota found a plausible connection between rates of newspaper circulation and voter turnout for that area. Local journalism has long been attributed to increasing votership and creating a greater community understanding of local politics and elections. 'News and information from local sources about our communities and community institutions help us to trust and understand our world and our place in the world. It is a terrible irony that as the ability to communicate information increases, our ability to know and trust the sources of communication has precipitously decreased,' said Carrie Woerner, D–Saratoga, Assembly sponsor of the bill. 'Whether small towns or big cities, New Yorkers need local journalism to reliably monitor and report on uniquely local concerns from school board policy and the actions of municipal boards to the volunteer organizations and activities that enrich our lives.' Woerner and Hoylman-Sigal had previously introduced the Local Journalism Sustainability Act together in 2021, but it died in the Assembly's Ways and Means Committee, and the Senate's Budget and Revenue committee. 'Our coalition's unprecedented mobilization of more than 150 New York local news outlets in just a few months sent a clear message to Albany: it's time to support local journalism,' said Zachary Richner, one of The Empire State News Coalition's founders in a statement. The bill was included in the Senate and Assembly's one-house budgets that were released on March 11, providing hope that the bipartisan legislation will be passed this time around. 'All New Yorkers deserve to have their voices heard, and hometown newspapers are key to that mission. We urge government officials and local stakeholders to rally behind us, safeguarding democracy and bolstering the future of local journalism in New York,' added Richner.

title: Assembly GOP Bill Package Would Increase Availability, Reduce Costs of Child Care
author: MARIAH PARMETER
description: On Monday March 11, Assembly Republicans introduced an 'Affordable Blueprint for Childcare.' The proposed legislation would expand access to early childcare education, create more affordability,…
content:
Legislative Gazette photo
Assemblyman Will Barclay stands at the podium joined by Assemblyman Ed Ra (left) and Assemblyman Josh Jensen (right) in support of legislation that would bolster childcare access and affordability in New York State. On Monday March 11, Assembly Republicans introduced an 'Affordable Blueprint for Childcare.' The proposed legislation would expand access to early childcare education, create more affordability, increase the number of childcare providers, and increase tax incentives for childcare providers and families. The Republican Conference stressed they believe childcare is not a Democrat or Republican issue, but a collective concern for all New Yorkers. While no bill in this proposed legislation has been picked up in the Senate, the legislation has many co-sponsors supporting it within the Assembly. There is an affordability crisis for day care statewide. Assemblyman Matt Slater, R-Yorktown, noted that paying child care for his own two children was like taking a second mortgage on his home. 'Fact of the matter is, we were paying a second mortgage for day care,' Slater said. The first thing this legislation will be doing is trying to uncover the issues established in the system currently ( A.8969 ) and to alleviate some of the cost for families ( A.9220 ), ( A.9257 ), ( A.9242 ). In total the conference believes their legislation could save the average family in New York State around $2,300 a year, which for some is desperately needed. 'The cost of childcare is three times higher than what can reasonably be afforded' said Assemblyman Edward Ra, R-Franklin Square. Assembly Minority Leader Will Barclay, R-Pulaski stated that childcare averages $16,000 a year for New York State parents, which is the sixth highest in the nation. 'It was easier for me to stay home and live on the system, than it was for me to go and work a full time job' says Kaysie Horwedel , mother of three who was invited to speak about her struggle finding affordable childcare. Even with a college degree Horwedel doesn't bring home $1,000 a week, which is what she was spending on daycare for all three children. The Assembly Republican bills would also expand the learning tools and facilities at childcare properties, along with increasing the number of providers for those facilities. Creating a list of providers for day care facilities to use in case of emergencies is a crucial step to help the already stressed and understaffed providers ( A.6071 ). 'When you set up a child for success, you help remove them from the cycle of poverty,' said Horwedel. A lot of facilities do not have the adequate resources to make each child with individual needs equally cared for especially when it comes to learning objectives. Part of this legislation is specifically incentivizing providers to update facilities ( A.9264 ), ( A.9245 ). Another important step in helping parents find care for their children is the advancement of normal day care hours to create non-traditional hours for parents and guardians who may not work the traditional nine-to-five job ( A.9126 ). Lastly the bill will tackle childcare affordability for not only the parents but also the facilities that are providing the care by using tax incentives and establishing the use of learning pod and pre-kindergarten education, ( A.9202 ), ( A.8579 ), ( A.9128 ). The expansion of collaboration requirements for Universal Pre-kindergarten Aid (UPK) will hopefully increase the number of students that these programs can serve. 'One of the happiest days my wife and I had was when we had UPK come into town,' joked Assemblyman Josh Jensen, R-Greece. 'I f we don't offer child care options for working parents, we have an entire aspect of our economy that's off limits to those who don't have people to keep their children safe.' Creating a safe place that parents can entrust their children to be therefore being able to work and be a part of the economy is an incredibly important task. Assemblyman Ra calls on the federal government to reinstate enhanced tax credit, that would expand and increase the earned income tax credit to 45% of a taxpayer's federal earned income tax credit ( A.9258 ). This would in turn incentivize taxpayers to keep working.
