Legislative Gazette file photo
An analysis of polling site data by the New York Public Interest Research Group finds that 20 four-year colleges in New York state have no polling place within a mile of campus.
With just weeks until the general election, the analysis shows that these large-population colleges — with on-campus housing and more than 1,000 full-time students — do not have a polling place within a mile from the campus. This can make it very difficult for young voters to participate in the election, especially if they do not have a means of transportation, according to the good-government groups.
In 2022, New York initiated an important new program to help young adults attending college to more easily vote. The law stated that campuses with 300 or more registered voters living on campus and registered at their college address should have a polling place.
'College students must be able to cast their ballots on their campus, as required by state law,' said Susan Lerner, executive director of Common Cause New York. 'In just a few weeks, New Yorkers — some for the first time — will vote in consequential elections across the state. We should be encouraging students to get involved, not shutting them out of the process.
'Local Election Commissioners must add more poll sites on college campuses before early voting starts.'
In their initial analysis before the primary in May, NYPIRG found 97 colleges with student housing but no poll site on campus and 26 colleges, including community colleges, with on-campus housing and more than 1,00 students but no polling site within a mile.
In 2022, New York passed a bill, S.4658/A.454, sponsored by Senator Kevin S. Parker and Assemblywoman Nily Rozic, meant to take effect in January 2024, that requires college campuses with 300 or more registered voters to have poll sites on campus property or in a site approved by the university.
The bill states, 'This bill recognizes the fact that requiring residents of colleges and universities to vote at sites remote from their campuses…can present unnecessary obstacles to voting.'
Given the size of the 20 four-year colleges NYPIRG investigated , they should have all been eligible for a polling site. Since May, only Buffalo State and Geneseo have added polling sites on their campuses.
Blair Horner, executive director of NYPIRG, said, 'Students too often face barriers to voting, and placing poll sites far off campus further dampens turnout among young voters. New Yorkers have a constitutional right to vote, policymakers should be reducing obstacles to voting, not increasing them.'
In a letter sent to members of the state Board of Elections, one can see that polling places are at least a mile or so away from campuses all over the state, from Rochester to West Point to Staten Island.
NYPIRG is asking state Board of Elections commissioners to explain how the law requiring a polling place on or contiguous to college campuses with 300 or more registered voters is being applied in these 20 campuses they identified. The watchdog group is also requesting under the Freedom of Information Law any communications and documents related to the decisions to not include polling places on the campuses listed below.
According to John Carroll University , young voters make up 21 percent of the voting eligible population in the U.S. Share America writes, 'In the most recent presidential election, in 2020, young voters were responsible for 17 percent of all votes cast, according to Tufts University experts.'
Younger college voters also form a more culturally diverse picture of America; they are more likely to be people of color, of diverse gender identities, part of the LGBTQ+ community, and so on. If they face obstacles in voting, due to the lack of convenient polling places, they may be unable to participate in their elections and their vital voices will not be heard.
Erica Smitka, executive director of the League of Women Voters of New York State, said, 'Voting has long been a challenge for college students due to transportation issues, scheduling conflicts, and a lack of information about the voting process. While recent legislation aimed to facilitate voting for New York's 1.1 million college-age students, we have yet to see significant increases in on-campus polling locations.
'By ensuring that these sites are conveniently located, we can empower students to actively engage in the democratic process.'

title: Harris Wins New York by 12-Point Margin, Hochul to Speak About Results Today at 1 P.M.
description: According to unofficial results compiled by the New York State Board of Elections, nearly 55 percent of New York voters cast a ballot for Vice President Kamala Harris while just over 43 percent voted…
content:
Photo by Susan Watts, courtesy of the Governor's Office
November 5, 2024 — Manhattan, NY — Governor Kathy Hochul holds a meeting with public safety officials to ensure election integrity at polling sites across New York.
According to unofficial results compiled by the New York State Board of Elections, nearly 55 percent of New York voters cast a ballot for Vice President Kamala Harris while just over 43 percent voted for former President Donald Trump.
New York's only ballot proposition — a constitutional amendment that would guarantee equal protection for New Yorkers regardless of race, color, ethnicity, national origin, age, disability, creed, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, or pregnancy status — passed 57 to 35 percent.
Nearly 3 million New York voters took part in early voting this year , which is about half a million more than voted early in the 2020 presidential election.
Gov. Kathy Hochul will deliver remarks on the election results today at 1 p.m. The speech will be livestreamed on the governor's website .
The State Board of Elections has tallied votes in 13,077 of 13,357 statewide election districts as of 8 a.m. on Nov. 6.

title: Assemblyman Alex Bores Wins Rising Star Award
author: JANANI HARIRAM
description: State Assemblyman Alex Bores received a Rising Star Award this week from the Future Caucus, which promotes a bipartisan political culture rooted in empathy and solutions for Gen Z and millennial…
content:
Photo courtesy of the Future Caucus
New York Assemblyman Alex Bores, at podium, accepts the 2024 Future Caucus Rising Star Award alongside fellow recipient, Senator-elect Tory Blew of Kansas.
State Assemblyman Alex Bores received a Rising Star Award this week from the Future Caucus, which promotes a bipartisan political culture rooted in empathy and solutions for Gen Z and millennial lawmakers.
Bores, a Manhattan Democrat, was awarded the seventh annual Rising Star Award , intended to recognize Gen Z and millennial state lawmakers who embody the organization's mission to transcend political tribalism by driving innovative, bipartisan legislation. The awards ceremony took place Thursday, November 21, at the Arlo Hotel in Washington D.C.
The Future Caucus also presented its Generational Changemaker Award to activist and actor Sophia Bush, for her efforts to promote voter education and civic engagement, and to businesswoman and socialite Paris Hilton, for her commitment to criminal justice reform and accountability for youth residential facilities.
'I'm honored to receive this award for work that prioritizes delivering results for New Yorkers,' Bores said. 'Creating a more effective, responsive state government requires everyone, and I'm proud of what we have achieved together to modernize New York's services and protect our democracy.'
Bores represents the 73rd District of New York in Manhattan, which includes the Upper East Side and Midtown East. He is a fifth-generation New Yorker, born and raised in the area he now represents.
He graduated with honors from Cornell and received a master's in Computer Science from Georgia Tech, working as an engineer before taking public office. According to his State Assembly Biography , however, the best education he ever received was on the picket line with his dad when he was eight years old while his dad's union was locked out for fighting for better health care.
The Future Caucus recognized his bipartisan efforts to modernize New York. In particular, his bill, A.8435/S.8572 , that aims to educate state agencies on the benefits of using cloud service providers and encourages them to use cloud computing to provide cheaper and more secure government services to New Yorkers.
'New Yorkers deserve fast, efficient, and secure service,' Bores said. 'The federal government and private sector companies are increasingly using cloud computing in order to provide flexibility and serve people better.'
His bill A.7106-B/S.6638-B enacted the 'political artificial intelligence disclaimer (PAID) act' that requires political communications to disclose when they are using artificial intelligence (AI) and maintain records about the usage of such synthetic material.
Bores, who was elected to the Assembly in 2022, said, 'There has been an increase in election disinformation designed to suppress voter turnout, misinform voters, undermine public trust in the electoral process: and AI technology can be used to create convincing, yet false images, video, and audio that can be used to manipulate public opinion.'
Bores supports the safe use of AI and transparency with viewers to maintain election safety and honesty.
His constituency engagement record additionally makes him a great candidate for the award. During two years in office, his office has resolved more than 300 constituent cases and hosted numerous 'mobile office hours' at libraries, public parks, and subway stops, easily accessible to New Yorkers and open to solving their everyday problems.
Bores co-chairs the New York Future Caucus with Assemblyman Ed Ra, a Long Island Republican elected to the Assembly in 2010.
Future Caucus president and CEO Layla Zaidane said, 'As founding co-chair of the New York Future Caucus, Assembly Member Bores sets a powerful example of how great leadership enables effective governing and bipartisan progress. Through his vision and drive, he's achieved big legislative wins while building a political culture of collaboration that's sparking positive change across the state'
She went on to say, 'As a fellow New Yorker, I couldn't be more proud to recognize Assembly Member Bores with this honor. His work embodies the very essence of Future Caucus — leadership, innovation, and true bipartisanship at its best.'

title: "One Fair Wage" Bill Would End Subminimum Pay for Restaurant Workers
author: Olivia Shults
description: New York lawmakers have reintroduced a bill to end the two-tier wage system for tipped workers, which often leads to a subminimum wage for specifically food industry workers. These workers have been…
content:
Legislative Gazette photos by Sean Ward
From left, Bill sponsors Sen. Robert Jackson and Assemblymember Jessica González-Rojas speak to supporters in the State Capitol on Monday, January 27 about the One Fair Wage bill. The bill aims to end the subminimum wage system that faces tipped workers in the hospitality industry.
New York lawmakers have reintroduced a bill to end the two-tier wage system for tipped workers, which often leads to a subminimum wage for specifically food industry workers.
These workers have been left out of similar legislation previously, such as a bill from five years ago that resulted in the end of a separate wage for tipped workers in almost every field, except the hospitality industry.
Assemblymember Jessica González-Rojas acknowledged that restaurant workers have been left out of the fight for higher wages in recent legislative sessions.
'We need to ensure that we uplift our workers,' she said.
Sen. Robert Jackson and González-Rojas backed the group One Fair Wage in launching a campaign on Monday, January 27 at the Capitol to support their bill ( S.415-a / A.1200 ).
Many argue that the instability of income and increase in the cost of living are making affordability for daily needs difficult. Assemblymember Claire Valdez argues that there is value in a stable income and that 'minimum wage is the floor, subminimum wage is the basement.'
Malika Henderson, a bartender of 11 years, said 'The cost of living is so high, it's a crisis.' She discussed her experience of having her car repossessed as a result of her relying on tips to make her car payments. She also spoke of the danger that can follow when you rely on tips for your livelihood.
'They are not anecdotes,' Sen. Jackson said. 'They are the lived realities of hundreds of thousands of Americans… My message is clear, I am on the side of fairness, dignity, and better wages,' he added.
Food service workers who earn tips in New York City, Westchester County, and Long Island make a minimum of $11 an hour, and $10.35 an hour in the remainder of the state. The tips received are expected to make up the difference between the base pay and the minimum wage of $16.50 in New York City, Westchester County, and on Long Island, and $15.50 elsewhere. In some cases, this gap is not filled by tips and by law, the restaurant must fill it. The unpredictability of income leaves many wondering what they are going to make each week.
'Small businesses are essential to the economy of New York,' said Freddy Castiblanco, owner of Terraza 7, a live music and art hub in Elmhurst, Queens. Castiblanco provides full minimum wage with tips on top to his employees and believes that everyone deserves that right. Legislative Gazette photo by Sean Ward
The tipped workers displayed an effigy of President Donald Trump to represent the corporate opposition to the One Fair Wage bill.
The legislation would increase the minimum wage for food industry workers earning tips, increasing yearly until it corresponds with the minimum wage. This would be met by a deadline of 2029 for New York City and its suburbs, and 2030 for the rest of the state.
Concerning the four-year plan that is being proposed, González-Rojas says that the annual increase in wages over the span of four years will help the restaurant industry ease into the change. She made a point to be clear they are not eliminating tips, and that tips are meant to be gratuitous, 'not something you depend on to feed your family or pay your rent,' she added.
The sponsors of the bill said that it would not eliminate tipping, but rather it would change the culture of it. Rojas supports that it would be more of a gratuitous gesture, rather than leaving workers with a dependence on tips to live.
Some pose the concern that eliminating a lower minimum wage for food service workers who receive tips would discourage customers from tipping at all. In addition, restaurant owners may have to raise menu prices to accommodate the increased minimum wage for tipped food service employees. The bill has the ability to change more than just the minimum wage for these workers, it could affect meal prices and sizes, as well as the amount of consumers eating out.
'This is not an attack on restaurant owners… it is an investment in the future of the industry,' said Sen. Jackson.
He went on to explain that New York must see this as an opportunity, and posed a question to Governor Hochul; 'Do you stand with the workers?' He then opened the question to the people of New York; 'If you were in their place, wouldn't you be standing here too?'

title: Hochul Promises $4.9M for Housing and Child Care in Schenectady
author: MATT GARTON
description: On Tuesday, January 28, Gov. Kathy Hochul announced a plan at SUNY Schenectady to award the Schenectady Community Action Program (SCAP) with a $4.9 million state grant. SCAP assists Schenectady…
content:
Photo by Darren McGee, courtesy of the Governor's Office
January 28, 2025 — Schenectady, NY — Gov. Kathy Hochul announces new investments of more than $100 million for projects located in certified Pro-Housing Communities, part of a total $123 million allocated as part of the latest round of the State's Regional Economic Development Council initiative.
On Tuesday, January 28, Gov. Kathy Hochul announced a plan at SUNY Schenectady to award the Schenectady Community Action Program (SCAP) with a $4.9 million state grant.
SCAP assists Schenectady families facing poverty, providing them with safe and affordable housing and child care. This grant will contribute toward building a SCAP Campus in the city of Schenectady. The SCAP Campus will be used to house a child care center, program space, and administrative offices to host a broad range of family support services.
'What they're taking is a vacant lot and turning it into a neighborhood hub with housing that's affordable and child care,' Hochul said. 'That's the power of this program.'
This project is a part of Hochul's bigger goal to award certified Pro-Housing Communities with more than $100 million this year for building new housing statewide.
Hochul's Pro-Housing Communities initiative provides funds for municipalities that promise to build new homes and invest in critical infrastructure projects, such as water and sewer system upgrades. This initiative allocates up to $650 million each year and distributes among 273 communities across New York, including Schenectady.
'So we're going to put together a fund in our budget that'll help local communities be able to envision what they want to do, put it on paper, and put together a plan that'll be successful,' Hochul said. 'That's how you build communities from the bottom up.'

title: Faith Leaders, Environmental Groups Supporting Two Bills Aimed at Reducing Plastic Packaging and Waste
author: JAMIE CASE
description: Faith leaders, environmental groups and elected officials met in Albany to 'put people over plastic' and show support for the Packaging Reduction and Recycling Infrastructure Act (S.1464/A.1749). The…
content:
Legislative Gazette photo by Nick Guercio
The Rev. Kathryn Beilke speaks to a crowd of bottle bill supporters in the state Capitol on January 28.
Faith leaders, environmental groups and elected officials met in Albany to 'put people over plastic' and show support for the Packaging Reduction and Recycling Infrastructure Act ( S.1464 / A.1749 ). The bill shifts the responsibility of recycling from municipalities to companies that produce plastic products.
It calls upon companies with annual net incomes exceeding $1 million that sell or distribute certain plastic products, to commit to sustainability. The bill, sponsored in the Senate by Environmental Conservation Committee Chair Pete Harkham, D-South Salem, would incrementally cut plastic packaging by 30 percent over 12 years and phase out harmful chemicals such as PFAS and vinyl chloride. It seeks to increase recyclability and reduce greenhouse gas emissions from plastic, which are projected to surpass coal-related emissions by 2030. The bill also imposes a new fee on packaging producers, with funds directed to local governments.
Four other states — Maine, Oregon, Colorado and California — have passed similar laws. More than 150 organizations and businesses — including Beyond Plastics, Consumer Reports, the League of Women Voters, Environmental Advocates, the New York Public Interest Research Group, Food and Water Watch, and the American Lung Association — issued a memo of support for the bills.
Sponsored in the Assembly by Environmental Conservation Committee Chair Deborah Glick, D-Greenwich Village, the Packaging Reduction and Recycling Infrastructure passed in the Senate but not in the Assembly during the last session. Building upon previous momentum, sponsors have high hopes for the bill's future success.
The coalition is also pushing an expanded bottle deposit law in New York, with legislation expected to be introduced by Glick and Sen. Rachel May, D-Syracuse.
The 'Bigger Better Bottle Bill' would build on the 1982 law by expanding the types of beverage containers eligible for a refundable deposit and aims to raise the fee to a dime. The decades-old nickel deposit designed to encourage recycling in the state may be losing effectiveness, with redemption rates falling below 70 percent in 2024. The deposit was first introduced in 1983, but proponents say it no longer serves as a strong incentive for recycling. The bill comes after Connecticut raised its bottle deposit to 10 cents and has seen recycling rates soar above 90 percent.
When the program was first introduced, unclaimed deposits helped reduce litter and landfill waste. However, changes in state policy now allocate 80 percent of unclaimed redemption funds to the state, leaving only 20 percent for distributors to manage operations. Last year, unclaimed deposits totaled $125 million. Advocates argue that a fairer distribution of funds is essential for long-term sustainability.
For redemption center operators, stagnant pay rates are a growing concern. Jess Amidon, the owner of two redemption centers said, 'We've been earning the same rates since 2009, though payroll costs have doubled and living expenses have risen 13 times.' The financial strain has forced about 25 percent of the state's redemption centers to close permanently over the past two years. Legislative Gazette photo by Nick Guercio
Environmental activists, bottle bill sponsors, and redemption center owners flood the million-dollar-staircase with examples of single use plastic to make a point about wasteful packaging.
While the original Bottle Bill passed 40 years ago garnered success, officials argue that the bill needs updating as plastic production and consumption changes. NYPIRG Senior Policy Advisor Blair Horner said 'It's 2025 and time for an update. The DEC knows it, the redemption centers that actually deal with returning the bottles know it and the canners who rely on returning bottles for income know it.'
Advocates made their way up the Million-Dollar Staircase in the State Capitol, and a multi-faith coalition of New Yorkers created a literal 'sea of plastic.' Dangling Amazon packaging, Tostitos bags and other single-use plastic from the top of the staircase they shared the message: 'New York is not disposable.'
Advocates are urging lawmakers to make the state's recycling programs a formal budget line item, citing the large sums it handles annually. Interfaith Coordinator for 'Beyond Plastics' Kathryn Beilke said, 'We have seen corporate voluntary pledges to reduce plastic packaging fail miserably. If we are to do anything about this global crisis for vulnerable communities, for our health, for our climate, we have to legislate solutions that limit the proliferation of single use packaging.'
The Business Council of New York State and other industry groups oppose the Packaging Reduction and Recycling Infrastructure Act, calling it overly restrictive compared to similar laws in Oregon and Washington. They warn it could raise consumer costs by over $1 billion annually, disproportionately affecting low-income households. According to Vice President Ken Pokalsky, the bill ignores most industry suggestions.
Jamie Case is an undergraduate student at SUNY New Paltz, with expertise in a myriad of media realms. When she's not producing content, she's chopping salads in a college town.

title: Roundtable Reveals More Details About Plans for Statewide School Phone Ban
author: KYLE BREDBERG
description: Gov. Kathy Hochul continues to push restricting smartphone use in schools statewide. The governor's plan would create a statewide standard for cell phone use during the school day, restricting the use…
content:
Legislative Gazette file photo
Gov. Kathy Hochul continues to push restricting smartphone use in schools statewide.
The governor's plan would create a statewide standard for cell phone use during the school day, restricting the use of smartphones for the entire day, including lunch and study hall.
'Kids are missing out on an education,' Hochul said. 'They're focusing more on memes instead of math and they're falling behind, because how could they not?'
According to Hochul's More Learning, Less Scrolling report, restricting student smartphone access improves student engagement in the classroom, communal areas and during extracurricular activities. The report also states it improves the mental health of both students and teachers.
Hochul sat at roundtables with high school students across New York state and posed questions about cellphone use in their schools. One question addressed the increasing pressure that school has on students because of social media.
Hochul posed a question to understand why students' are connected with their screens during the school day. '[The students] all said 'we can't stop ourselves'. One young woman said to me 'you have to save us from ourselves,' the governor said Thursday during a virtual chat with students and educators about distraction free schools.
The proposal would create a 'bell-to-bell' restriction on smartphone use on school grounds, requiring them to be stored with the school at the beginning of the day, and then returned at the end of the day.
As for how the phones are stored, that would be left up to the district. The governor's proposal requires each of New York's more than 800 school districts to develop its own plans for storing and securing smartphones and has allotted $13.5 million in funding for storage solutions, including cubbies and pouches.
Not all devices will have to be stored away. In a recent news release, Hochul specifically mentions smartphones and 'internet-enabled personal devices,' are the only ones required to be stored away. Cellphones and other devices that cannot connect to the internet would be allowed.
School districts will also be able to tailor individual policies based on their views of how technology, such as laptops, will benefit the student body. Other exceptions to the cell phone ban proposal include if a student needs a device to manage healthcare, translation, or any other education accommodations. Photo by Mike Groll, courtesy of the Governor's Office
January 22, 2025 – Guilderland, NY – Gov. Kathy Hochul launches her statewide push for distraction-free schools at Farnsworth Middle School in Guilderland, Albany County.
Without access to smartphones, parents may be concerned about their children's safety in an emergency. The governor's view opposes the concern, explaining in the proposal report that schools have crafted policies designed to restore phone access in an emergency situation, and even hiring additional staff to field calls from parents who need to be i touch with their children.
New York State Police Superintendent Steven James believes that keeping students and their phones separated during an emergency will lead to better security outcomes.
'The use of mobile phones by students during a quickly developing school emergency is a distraction that could compromise the safety of the students and school staff,' James stated in Hochul's news release.
The governor believes these policy changes will substantially impact the experiences of students, leading to a more engaged student body.
'This won't be easy, but as a mom, I know we have to make the tough decisions to do what's right for our kids,' Hochul said. 'We're going to make sure there's no smart phones, no watches, no tablets, no beeps or dings in that sacred space, from the bell in the morning to the bell in the afternoon.
'I need to help these young people and start changing the culture, so you are the last generation that has to feel this addiction,' said Hochul.

title: Domestic Violence Service Providers Hope Legislature Will Help Stabilize Programs And Services For Victims
author: KYLE VAN BELL
description: The New York State Coalition Against Domestic Violence is urging the Assembly and Senate to include a $200 million appropriation in their upcoming one-house budget bills, aimed at improving the…
content:
Legislative Gazette photos by Myanoe Aung
The New York State Coalition Against Domestic Violence is urging the Assembly and Senate to include a $200 million appropriation in their upcoming one-house budget bills, aimed at improving the efficiency of delivering services to those in need.
According to Joan Gerhardt, the director of public policy and advocacy for the organization, nearly 200 domestic violence advocates attended the event, one of the biggest turnouts they have ever had. She highlighted the problem that more than 90 percent of the state's funding for domestic violence services is federal.
'Our work is vulnerable to the whims of Washington,' she said.
The Coalition Against Domestic Violence was established in 1978 and is the designated point of contact and resource center for domestic violence in New York. It is responsible for supporting the enhancement of domestic violence intervention and prevention.
Currently, only 0.079 percent of the state budget is being allocated to domestic violence services. This concern is not specific to NYSCADV and domestic violence support programs, but many nonprofits in New York state. According to Megan Allen, the CEO of the New York Council of Nonprofits Inc., 65 percent of nonprofits are concerned about funding basic operations. This concern stems from not having enough funding to pay their workers, as 'revenues barely cover the costs of living,' Allen said. 'We are competing against Burger King for workers and we are losing.'
'At the heart of the crisis is federal funding dependence,' said Kellyann Kostyal-Lerrier, executive director of Fearless Hudson Valley Incorporated, formerly known as Safe Homes of Orange County.
Kostyal-Lerrier also explained the current staffing crisis that shows extremely low employment numbers for domestic violence services, which was caused by a lack of workers due to dramatically low wages and inadequate funding. She added that there were even instances where 'an unprecedented amount of funds were left on the table due to a lack of workers. '
Senator Roxanne Persaud, D-Canarsie, also addressed the staffing issue, urging that domestic violence service workers deserve to be recognized for their work. 'Too often domestic violence workers are seen as not important,' she said.
Another common problem discussed was the lack of understanding for the victims of domestic violence. This is one aspect that the Domestic Violence Services Transformation and Stabilization Program aims to improve upon. 'The voices of the survivors are on the forefront of advocacy and liberation,' said Assemblymember Jessica Gonzalez-Rojas, D-Jackson Heights.
The $200 million proposed program focuses on shifting reliance from federal to state funding to provide greater flexibility for domestic violence programs and NYSCADV. It aims to reduce the number of state agencies overseeing funding, streamlining the contracting process for service providers while cutting administrative costs. Most funding would be distributed through non-competitive grants without match requirements, easing financial burdens on rural and more varied cultural communities.
The proposal also removes county Departments of Social Services from contracting responsibilities, allows for upfront and timely payments to providers, and enhances culturally responsive services to better support unserved and underserved communities. Legislative Gazette photo by Myanoe Aung
Assemblymembers Linda Rosenthal and Andrew Hevesi spoke at the event as they both sponsor legislation that the group favors, sharing the same concerns and aspects of their plans for solutions. Rosenthal, D-Upper West Side, covered her proposed bill that aims to ensure that any survivors of domestic violence who have debts that they are not responsible for will not be held liable.
Assemblyman Hevesi, D-Forest Hills, spoke about his plan to finally establish Kyra's Law, which has been discussed for more than five years but never made official. Kyra Franchetti was murdered by her father during a court-approved, unsupervised visit, despite warnings and accounts of abusive behavior. Kyra was 28 months old at the time of the case, which occurred in 2016.
Kyra's Law aims to help prevent children from abuse at the hands of their parents/caregivers. Hevesi described it as 'the most complicated legislation' he's ever worked on, but pledges to get it done in 2025. The bill ( A.6194 ) was introduced to the Assembly Judiciary Committee on Thursday, February 27. A companion bill ( S.5998 ), sponsored by Sen. James Skoufis, D-Cornwall, was introduced in the Senate Judiciary Committee on March 4.
Hevesi also addressed the staffing issue and that domestic violence services aren't alone in suffering from low wages, adding that 'our entire state is behind on paying the workforce,' he said.
The domestic violence service workforce has been stretched thin, but the need for their services has only increased. 'The workers that are still left are picking up the work,' said Kostyal-Lerrier. 'We are the ones, there's no one else coming … we have to stay in the fight.'

title: Newark middle schooler brings airline deregulation presentation to National History Day contest
author: Emma Baum
description: Inspired by her and her grandfather's shared love of travel, Appleman chose to create a website about the Airline Deregulation Act of 1978 and its impact on commercial aviation for her project submission.
content:
While most 14-year-olds were enjoying a few extra hours of sleep and spending the afternoon at the local pool, Alaina Appleman spent the second week of her summer break presenting original research to a panel of judges at the National History Day Contest at the University of Maryland, College Park.
Currently in its 50th year, National History Day is a nonprofit organization that aims to improve teaching and learning of history at the middle and high school levels through student-led historical inquiry and research. Students across the country, as well as in regions ranging from Puerto Rico to South Korea, develop a research topic with relevance to the annual theme; this year, it was 'Turning Points in History.' After conducting initial research on their chosen topic, students then decide which of five presentation options – documentary, exhibit, paper, performance, or website – would best fit the story they are trying to tell.
When the time came to choose a topic for her History Day project in Stacey Smith's eighth-grade social studies class at St. Francis de Sales School in Newark last December, Appleman didn't have to think too hard. The oldest grandchild of Paul Kaparoff, who spent over 30 years in airline management, Appleman has grown up tagging along on trips that have taken her everywhere from France to Australia. Inspired by her and her grandfather's shared love of travel, Appleman chose to create a website about the Airline Deregulation Act of 1978 and its impact on commercial aviation for her project submission.
'For all my other projects I had to do, like for Science Fair, I chose to do boards, and they're sort of boring,' said Appleman of her decision to present a website rather than the more traditional exhibit board or academic paper. 'You don't get to have fun with it and design it. But when you do a website, you get to choose the font and design all the colors.'
Both the Science Fair and National History Day are staples of the seventh and eighth grade curriculum at St. Francis de Sales, where Appleman was a student. Students are required to do a research project during both years of junior high; those who compete in the Science Fair in seventh grade must compete in National History Day in eighth grade and vice versa.
'What we encourage is for them to become an expert on their topic,' said Smith, who has been the junior high social studies and religion teacher at St. Francis for 39 years. She estimates that she has been doing National History Day with her students for at least 30 years. 'A lot of times students aren't in a situation where they feel like they are the expert. But I think this project challenges [them] to grow in all of those areas.'
After receiving feedback on her project from judges at the local History Day fair, Appleman was named a state qualifier in the Junior Individual Website category at the regional competition hosted by Ohio History Connection on March 9. On April 20, Appleman took first place in the category at the state level, securing her advancement to the national contest.
Smith attributes the successes to Appleman's ability to apply feedback and adapt her project as necessary.
'She really listened to what the judges and the teachers said and made her project better all the time,' said Smith.
Appleman is her first student to advance to the National Contest. 'She also chose something she loved. At every level, there's interviews by the judges. And so if you love what you're doing, I think that comes across in your interview.'
While Appleman did not place at the national contest, the experience – from research to representing the state on a national stage – has certainly made an impact.
'I've loved watching her confidence grow,' said Laura Appleman, Alaina's mother. 'She's very mature, and I can't wait to see what she does with her life, because I think she's destined for pretty amazing things, and she's just a hard worker. My husband and I just are in awe of the passions that she has.'
Appleman might be just entering high school, but she can already see herself pursuing history in the future. It's an interest that has been informed by the passion of those who came before her.
'It's amazing how history is instilled from generations,' said Laura Appleman. '[My dad] showed the importance of travel and experiencing the world to my sister and I, and then he's made sure to do that same thing with his grandkids.'
While the national contest winners were announced just days ago on June 13, National History Day has already announced the theme for next year's contest, which Appleman is considering entering. For the next few months, though, she's looking forward to taking a break and enjoying life in the present.

title: State Police, Gov. Hochul meet with college administrators to prepare for possible campus protests this fall
author: RYAN CARRION
description: After widespread protests on college campuses last spring, Gov. Kathy Hochul and State Police met with campus leaders from more than 200 colleges and universities in late August to discuss college…
content:
Photos by Mike Groll, courtesy of the Governor's Office
August 26, 2024 – Albany, NY – Gov. Kathy Hochul convenes a virtual meeting with college leaders, State Police and other officials on campus safety for the fall semester.
After widespread protests on college campuses last spring, Gov. Kathy Hochul and State Police met with campus leaders from more than 200 colleges and universities in late August to discuss college safety and new emergency procedures.
Some of those attending the meeting were public safety experts to reinforce the importance of having an emergency plan. State Police and the Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Services were among those who met with college officials on August 26.
In anticipation of potential issues and protests during the fall 2024 semester, the State Police superintendent directed troop commanders across New York to visit with college administration at 'campuses of concern' prior to the beginning of the fall semester.
The troop commanders have been directed to discuss each college's stance on campus protests, their planned course of action in the event of protests and to get insight into the college's expectations of assistance from police.
'The safety and security of all New Yorkers remains our top priority and we have zero tolerance for any individuals that perpetuate hate crimes, acts of violence and harassment within our communities,' said New York State Police Superintendent Steven James. 'No student should ever feel vulnerable at their place of education.'
According to the Governor's Office, the State Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Services conducted reviews of emergency plans at individual college campuses and conducted training sessions with colleges this past summer.
'Public safety is my top priority, and as classes resume, it is essential that all students feel safe and are free from harm,' Gov. Hochul said on the day she met with college administrators in late August. 'Last spring, I directed college campuses to review and update their emergency response plans, and as tensions may be high as we start the academic year, I will continue to ensure all campus leaders and public safety officials have the resources they need to keep students safe.'
Colleges that are participating in these recent meetings and training sessions are in the SUNY and CUNY systems as well as private colleges affiliated with the Commission on Independent Colleges and Universities and the Association of Private Colleges.
According to City & State , there were protests on nearly a dozen New York college campuses last spring, including New York University, Columbia University, Cornell University, Syracuse University, SUNY Purchase, SUNY Stony Brook, The New School, The Fashion Institute of Technology, and SUNY New Paltz.
At SUNY New Paltz, State Police arrested 133 people on May 2, mostly students, creating an ongoing rift between campus leaders and a portion of the student body and faculty.
Gov. Hochul wrote a letter last spring semester to all colleges and universities in New York, reiterating the obligation these places of learning have to provide students an education in a safe environment under New York state's human rights laws and the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
Title VI of the Civil Rights Act prohibits discrimination based on race, color and national origin in programs and activities receiving federal financial assistance.
'At SUNY, safety is paramount and we have been and remain fiercely committed to ensuring security, civil discourse, and inclusivity on our campuses,' said SUNY Chancellor John King. 'We stand with Gov. Hochul in rejecting antisemitism, Islamophobia, and hatred and bigotry in any form.'
The State Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Services is advising campuses to use both the updated Emergency Response Plans and the Emergency Action Plans. This was all taken into consideration before the start of the Fall 2024 Semester to be better prepared after the events of late Spring.

title: Gov. Hochul Reviewing Her "Options and Obligations" Following Indictment of NYC Mayor
author: JANANI HARIRAM
description: New York City Mayor Eric Adams has been charged with bribery, campaign finance fraud, and conspiracy offenses following a lengthy investigation. Now, Gov. Kathy Hochul said she is reviewing her…
content:
Photo by Darren McGee, courtesy of the Governor's Office
New York City Mayor Eric Adams has been charged with bribery, campaign finance fraud, and conspiracy offenses following a lengthy investigation.
Now, Gov. Kathy Hochul said she is reviewing her options in the coming days to determine if she should remove Adams as mayor as he prepares for his criminal trial.
'This is an extraordinarily difficult day for New York City, ' Gov. Hochul said in a statement Thursday night. 'I have carefully reviewed the indictment released by the United States Department of Justice. This indictment is the latest in a disturbing pattern of events that has, understandably, contributed to a sense of unease among many New Yorkers.
'Our judicial system is based on the foundational principle that all of us are presumed innocent until proven otherwise. Yet those of us who have chosen a career in elected office know that we're held to a higher standard,' Hochul continued. 'Given the responsibilities we hold as public servants, that's entirely appropriate.
'New Yorkers deserve to know that their municipal government is working effectively, ethically and in the best interests of the people – driving down crime, educating our kids and ensuring basic city services continue unabated. It's now up to Mayor Adams to show the City that he is able to lead in that manner.
'My focus is on protecting the people of New York and ensuring stability in the city,' the governor continued. 'While I review my options and obligations as the governor of New York, I expect the Mayor to take the next few days to review the situation and find an appropriate path forward to ensure the people of New York City are being well-served by their leaders. We must give New Yorkers confidence that there is steady, responsible leadership at every level of government.'
For nearly a decade, Adams used his prominent positions in New York City government to obtain illegal campaign contributions and luxury travel, the indictment alleges. Adams solicited and accepted these benefits from foreign nationals, businessmen, and others, states the United States Attorney's Office . The most prominent of these foreign officials is a senior official in the Turkish diplomatic establishment, identified in the indictment as the Turkish Official.
Investigators said Adams sought illegal campaign funds for his 2021 mayoral campaign from The Turkish Official and other foreign wealthy businesspeople. Adams would provide favorable treatment in exchange. Adams used these illegal funds, straw contributions which were falsely certified to be donated by nominal donors while the true contributors hid their identity, to steal public funds.
New York City's Matching Funds Program serves to encourage candidates to engage New York residents, by matching small dollar contributions with public funds. It was intended to empower more candidates to run for office, even without access to wealthy contributors or supporters. Straw contributions, contributions from people who are not US citizens, contributions from foreign entities, and contributions from corporations are banned from the program, according to the indictment . Adams used his straw contributions to defraud New York City of more than $10,000,000.
For discounts when traveling using Turkey's national airlines, luxurious hotel rooms, free high-class meals, and other benefits, Adams agreed to construct the 36-story Turkish consular building without a fire inspection so that it could be ready in time for a visit by Turkey's president.
'We call on Mayor Adams to resign immediately. If he does not resign, we call on Governor Hochul to remove him from office using the powers granted her in Section 34 of the New York State Public Officers Law,' said the good-government group Reinvent Albany. 'Regardless of his ultimate guilt or innocence to the specific federal charges, we believe the extensive revelations of serious misdeeds by numerous people who work for the mayor, the indictment of the mayor himself, the resignation of top commissioners – including the heads of the police, schools, and health departments – have left Mayor Adams unable to effectively govern.'
New York State Conservative Party Chairman Gerard Kassar said, 'Governor Kathy Hochul has the power and obligation to remove New York City Mayor Eric Adams from office, following the near complete collapse of his administration under growing FBI probes.'
This is not the first time Adams has been accused of illegal conduct. In March of this year, a lawsuit was brought against Adams for sexually assaulting a woman in 1993 and demanding sexual favors from her. Adams vehemently denied these claims and stated that he did not know the woman.
Adams has been charged with one count of conspiracy, carrying a maximum sentence of 5 years in prison, one count of wire fraud, which carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison, two counts of soliciting campaign contributions from foreign nationals, which each carry a maximum sentence of 5 years in prison, and one count of soliciting a bribe, which carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison. Adams will be tried under U.S. District Judge Dale E. Ho.
FBI Assistant Director James E. Dennehy said: 'Today's indictment serves as a sobering moment but also sends a powerful message to every elected official in this country: public service is a profound responsibility, and it should be a noble calling. When that's perverted by greed and dishonesty, it robs us of our trust. This is a reminder that no one is above the law or beyond reproach.'
Ryan Carrion and James Gormley contributed to this report.

title: Housing, Economy and Immigration Among Top Issues for Voters in CD18
author: JANANI HARIRAM
description: NEW PALTZ, N.Y. — A new poll finds that 51 percent of voters in New York's 18th Congressional District support incumbent Democrat Pat Ryan, while 42 percent support Republican challenger Republican…
content:
Legislative Gazette photo by Patrick Kelly
NEW PALTZ, N.Y. — A new poll finds that 51 percent of voters in New York's 18th Congressional District support incumbent Democrat Pat Ryan, while 42 percent support Republican challenger Republican Alison Esposito. Seven percent are undecided.
Since earlier this month, Ryan's support has increased by three points, from 48 percent to 51 percent, while Esposito's support decreased by a point.
The poll — a collaboration between Emerson College, Pix11 and The Hill — has been tracking voter attitudes in Hudson Valley congressional districts, which are among the most expensive, closest and most hotly contested races this fall.
And even though Ryan holds the lead, the most recent poll shows Donald Trump beating Kamala Harris by 48.5 to 47.5 percent among voters who have decided. Pollsters found that 56.9 percent of the voters in CD18 disapprove of the job President Joe Biden is doing as president and 58.1 percent disapprove of the job Kathy Hochul is doing as governor of New York.
The Emerson College/PIX11?The Hill poll conducted in early and late October show that the most important issues for voters in the 18th Congressional District are the economy, housing affordability, immigration and threats to democracy.
Crime, health care and abortion access were also mentioned by voters when asked 'what is the most important issue facing New York?'
An October debate between Ryan and Esposito, and hosted by PIX11, touched on many of these topics, as well as the current conflict in the Middle East, New York's border control, gun laws, and military recruitment. Video courtesy of PIX11 News, via YouTube
One of the first questions posited to Esposito and Ryan focused on taxation and improving the economy.
Esposito said, 'Bidenomics is a failure' and supported energy diversification and lowering grocery prices.
Ryan supported raising taxes for top earners, saying 'Do we want to continue giving tax breaks to billionaires and corporations because of the Trump plan or are we going to finally make the ultra-wealthy pay their share?'
Henry Rosoff, the mediator of the debate, pointed out that housing prices in Ulster County rose by $66,000 between 2022 and 2024. Esposito said, 'The American dream is slipping away and we have to lower the price of everything.'
Both candidates were forced to confront high inflation and the current housing crisis in their district. According to the Emerson college poll, 48 percent of voters in the 18th Congressional District said they are worse off financially, compared to one year ago.
PIX11 political analyst J.C. Polanco said, in the post-show breakdown, 'Congressman Ryan had to step out of his comfort zone because it is the Democrats that run the White House and the U.S. Senate.' He was seen taking a more defensive position than Esposito.
Ryan's focus on abortion rights during his campaign led to the issue being stressed during the debate, though Esposito tried to move on from the topic. She said, 'I do not advocate for a federal abortion ban. Abortion is not on the ballot. It is protected in New York.'
However, Ryan brought up her support of the Life at Conception Act , a bill that stated that the right of life should be granted at each stage of life inclusive of fertilization. Esposito did not support the act in writing as Ryan claims, and she repeatedly stated that she would not remove any abortion protections in New York if elected. Video courtesy of PIX11 News, via YouTube
Given Ryan's military record and Esposito's previous career as an NYPD officer, the topic of gun control struck both personally.
Esposito said, 'We do not remove a Second Amendment right from our people just because someone committed a crime,' and vouched for punishing the individual rather than the tool of their violence. She additionally attacked Ryan's stance on the matter, saying 'My opponent, who is a defund the police guy, who has marched with BLM, calls even guns in the hands of cops weapons.'
After the debate, Ryan said, 'I was really disturbed actually to hear my opponent say we don't have a gun problem in the United States of America.'
On the controversial topic of Israel, both parties agreed on their support, though Esposito claimed that Ryan did not support Israel enough and had acted in ways that delayed ending the war, by calling for a ceasefire, for example. Esposito called Israel 'our greatest ally' and when asked if there was anything Israel could do to lose his support, Ryan responded, 'Not that I can think of.'
With some progressive voters angry about Israel's ongoing war with Palestine, Ryan could lose a number of voters with this stance. The NY-18 No Votes for Genocide is a campaign that encourages constituents to leave their ballots blank unless Ryan publicly calls for a federal arms embargo on Israel.
In the post-show analysis, J.C. Polanco, said 'We saw more of a detailed policy-talkish material coming out of Congressman Ryan and a much more spirited 'Our voters are angry they can't afford stuff' [coming from Esposito] and people respond to that, especially in a district like this.'
The Emerson College Polling/Pix11/The Hill New York 18th District poll was conducted October 24-26, 2024 among a sample of 450 likely voters. It has a credibility interval of 4.6 percentage points.

title: Watchdog Groups: Don't Change Election Laws Mid-Cycle
author: KYLE BREDBERG
description: After outrage from Republicans and some government watchdog groups, Democrats in the State Legislature are backing off a controversial proposal to change New York State Election Law, which would have…
content:
Legislative Gazette file photo
After outrage from Republicans and some government watchdog groups, Democrats in the State Legislature are backing off a controversial proposal to change New York State Election Law, which would have left Congresswoman Elise Stefanik's soon-to-be vacant seat in the House empty for months.
The legislation ( S.4588 / A.4881 ) sought to change how special elections are scheduled. Notably, it would amend the law so that if a special election is needed within the same year as a general election, the two would be held on the day of the general election in November.
Stefanik, R-Schuylerville, who was recently nominated by President Donald Trump to be the U.S ambassador to the United Nations, represents District 21, a staunchly Republican district and was serving her fifth term. If Stefanik is confirmed for the U.N. post, this legislation would have delayed the filling of that seat for months, shrinking the Republicans' slim majority in the House of Representatives from three seats to two.
The introduction of the proposal in both the state Senate and Assembly occurred last Friday evening, following a recent closed-door meeting , where Democratic lawmakers reportedly discussed changing the state's election laws.
'Democrats posted this legislation on a Friday evening like the cowards they are, hoping New Yorkers aren't paying attention to this electoral heist,' said Ed Cox, chair of the New York State Republican Committee, calling the proposal an antidemocratic power grab.
Assembly Minority Leader, Will Barclay R-Pulaski, expressed a similar sentiment.
'It's absolutely disgraceful that Democrats took this step,' barclay said. 'There is no justifiable reason to change the law and deliberately delay a special election in the 21st Congressional District. This needs to be investigated, litigated, and shut down by any means necessary.'
The bill would have changed the timeframe of special elections, reducing their urgency. Under current law, the governor has 10 days after a seat is vacated to declare a special election, and must conduct the special election between 70 and 80 days after it is declared.
The proposed legislation — introduced by Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins and Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie on Feb. 7 — would increase the time the governor has to declare an election to 15 days, and make the 70 to 80 day requirement only necessary if a general election is not being held in that same year.
Last week, Gov. Kathy Hochul defended her interest in changing election laws, stating a range of benefits that combining special and general elections could bring to New Yorkers. These included decreased cost and increased democratic engagement in elections, as the candidates in special elections are typically handpicked by their party bosses and county committees.
According to the bill, special elections increase voter confusion and fatigue by asking voters to participate in multiple elections throughout the year, decreasing voter turnout.
'We want to make sure that we get as many people to the poll, that we reduce as much chaos at least here, as possible as we consolidate things,' Stewart-Cousins said at a recent press conference.
On Feb. 7, Citizens Union and Reinvent Albany, two government watchdog organizations, sent a letter to Hochul , Stewart-Cousins, and Heastie expressing their concern over changing the state's Election Law 'midcycle.'
'The election cycle should not be subject to political manipulation. Changes to special elections rules should not take effect immediately,' stated the letter.
John Kaehny, executive director of Reinvent Albany, expanded on this point in an interview with The Legislative Gazette. 'A good analogy is to changing the rules of a football game during the game,' Kaehny said. 'The proposal to change the law in the middle of an election cycle is inherently, highly, highly political, and an attempt to create some type of advantage.'
The good-government groups believe the states' election laws can be improved.
In the letter , the two groups criticized the current structure of special elections, which lack traditional primaries.
'Currently special elections circumvent party primaries by using closed-door decisions in which party leadership chooses its nominee, and everyday New Yorkers are cut out of the process,' stated the letter.
Once elected, these officials, like all incumbents, tend to be reelected. According to a 2017 report provided by Citizens Union, at least 29 percent of the State Legislature has been elected through this process.
The letter urges the Legislature to make a change to this process, modeling the special election process after New York City, where candidates petition to be on the special election ballot and then are chosen through a non-partisan ranked choice vote.
'Competitive elections and real choices increase turnout far more than changes in the election timeline,' stated Reinvent Albany.
The proposed legislation does not make any changes to the structure of special elections other than changing the time they are held.
The letter also commends the Legislature for taking steps to consolidate elections, agreeing that doing so would increase the low voter turnout historically seen in special elections, but states that it needs to be done with care, so as to not leave a district unrepresented for an extended period.
The letter also emphasizes that the change should not happen during an election cycle.
'Changing election law mid-cycle to serve immediate political objectives undermines the principles of good governance.'

title: Amid Growing Safety Concerns, Republicans Ask Governor To Repeal The HALT Act
author: OLIVIA SHULTS
description: Amid statewide protests and walkouts by corrections officers, the Assembly Republican Conference held a press conference in the state Capitol on Monday, calling on Gov. Kathy Hochul to take immediate…
content:
Legislative Gazette file photo
Amid statewide protests and walkouts by corrections officers, the Assembly Republican Conference held a press conference in the state Capitol on Monday, calling on Gov. Kathy Hochul to take immediate action to restore order in state correctional facilities.
Following the inmate takeover at Collins Correctional Facility in Erie County, corrections officers across the state are protesting working conditions, understaffing, and the Humane Alternatives to Long-Term Solitary Confinement Act.
Barclay noted that three things are apparent surrounding these protests: the goal is not abut money, but rather the corrections officers' safety and quality of life; there is no easy political solution; and this current situation has been building for several years as a result of prison closures, staffing problems, and the HALT Act.
The HALT Act ( A.2277-a / S.2836 ) restricts the use of solitary confinement, limiting the duration of solitary confinement to a maximum of 15 days. In addition, it prohibits inmates over the age of 55, those under 21, pregnant inmates, and inmates with disabilities from being placed in solitary confinement.
Opponents of the HALT Act say it removes consequences for dangerous behavior and severely compromises the ability of officers to discipline inmates.
Since the HALT Act took effect on March 31, 2022, the Department of Corrections and Community Supervision has reported a 169 percent increase in assaults between inmates, a 76 percent increase in inmate on staff assaults, and a 32 percent increase in instances involving contraband.
Barclay and his fellow Republicans are calling on Gov. Hochul to include a repeal of the HALT Act in her 30-day budget amendments.
'The HALT Act looked great on paper to liberal Democrats who never spent a day working in prisons,' Barclay said 'But who has it protected? Prison violence has soared since it was implemented. Inmates are less safe. Correctional officers are less safe. The entire system has become more dangerous. We don't need another year of alarming violence to know what needs to be done.'
After visiting Auburn Correctional Facility and talking to protesting corrections officers, Barclay said 'frankly the corrections officers don't feel like anyone has their backs down here in Albany. The governor is going to have to show true leadership to solve this problem.'
Assemblyman Dave DiPietro, R-East Aurora, said the state correctional facilities are in a state of chaos and corrections officers are walking into a 'battlefield' every day. He added that they are overworked, understaffed, and left defenseless by Albany's 'reckless pro-criminal agenda,' calling the current state justice system a 'disgrace' as a result of failed policies.
Addressing Gov. Hochul, he said 'the time for excuses is over.'
Corrections officers across the state are overworked due to understaffing, sometimes being mandated 16-24 hour shifts. DiPietro noted that oftentimes due to the overworking of corrections officers, they return home unable to care for their families due to exhaustion and the mental instability resulting from the difficult working conditions.
The Assembly Republican last week also sent a letter to Gov. Hochul, chastising her announcing she plans to close up to five more prisons in the near future.
Assemblyman Phil Palmesano, R-Corning, discussed the effects of the combination of prison closures, a massive staffing shortage and policies that make correctional officers' jobs more difficult. Stating that this has 'created a powder keg environment inside state prisons… More corrections officers are retiring and resigning each year than are coming in.'
Members of the Assembly Minority Conference have been visiting with the corrections officers demonstrating outside of state correctional facilities, as well as their families and other supporters. In doing so, the feedback given by these individuals has signaled public unrest with systemic failures that ignore the safety and wellbeing of corrections officers, staff, and inmates.
With the conditions inside of prisons reaching extremes, Assembly Minority members are calling for a resolution to the ongoing crisis. Barclay and those standing beside him are calling for an immediate repeal of the HALT act before conditions continue to worsen.
Assemblyman Matt Simpson, R-Horicon, called attention to the risks corrections officers are taking by protesting, stating 'Where is the governor? Has she talked to the corrections officers that have so great of concern that they are willing to risk their jobs?'
Gov. Kathy Hochul has threatened the loss of health insurance and legal consequences against corrections officers who are walking off the job to demonstrate. By walking off the job, the lives of inmates and staff are being put at risk, and the employed corrections officers are violating the Taylor Law by doing so.
Hochul has deployed 6,500 members of the New York National Guard to replace the protesting corrections officers, helping with tasks including distributing meals and medication to incarcerated individuals and helping maintain general order and wellness in the facilities.
State officials have appointed a mediator and temporarily suspended portions of the HALT Act, which places limitations on solitary confinement. The Republican Conference has sided with the corrections officers, sympathetic to the effects of the HALT Act on the officers, staff, inmates, and their families.
Assemblyman Anil Beephan, R-East Fishkill, said that there was one common theme among meeting with various corrections officers, 'they loved their jobs prior to HALT.'

title: Advocates Say HALT Act, More Protections Needed for Prisoners' Safety
author: MIA QUICK
description: While hundreds of corrections officers rallied outside the state Capitol on Tuesday, a smaller group of prisoners' rights advocates stood on the fringes of the crowd, calling for a prison system that…
content:
Legislative Gazette photo by Mia Quick
While hundreds of corrections officers rallied outside the state Capitol on Tuesday, a smaller group of prisoners' rights advocates stood on the fringes of the crowd, calling for a prison system that protects the incarcerated along with the employees.
The smaller group of counter protesters from Jails Justice Network, an organization that attempts to reform corrections policy, stood a few feet away from the rally organized by corrections officers demanding better working conditions and a repeal of the controversial HALT Act .
After emerging from their own larger event inside the Capitol, the prisoner advocates held signs that read, 'brutality, rape, and murder are not in the job description,' 'incarcerated lives matter,' and 'Robert Brooks — say his name.' Brooks was an inmate who died a day after a beating he received from several corrections officers at Marcy Correctional Facility late last year. Body camera footage showed Brooks handcuffed and beaten in the facility.
The counter protesters said they fear what could happen to incarcerated individuals if the HALT Act is repealed, they want a system that will protect prisoners just as much as the guards. They shouted, 'enough is enough,' 'stop killing us,' and claimed that the strike was a slap in the face to Brooks. Legislative Gazette photo by Mia Quick
'I was handcuffed, shackled, and beaten,' said Thomas Kearney, formerly incarcerated and the co-organizer for the Jails Justice Network, and a former Prison Rape Elimination Act outreach director for the Coalition Against Sexual Assault. 'After, I was charged with aggravated assault.'
Kearney served 17 years in prison and said he suffered abuse at the hands of officers in his facility. After his beating, he said they charged him with aggravated assault and claimed he attempted the first hit. Kearney said he was simply walking out of his cell.
'We're talking about a system that people should be putting love at,' said Rory Smalls, a member of the Jails Justice Network, 'They want certain things removed to do sneaky things.'
At one point during the corrections officers rally, one of the prisoners rights protesters shouted and held up her sign at Michael Sussman, a lawyer and the main speaker, as he spoke. The corrections officers responded by booing her and covering or hitting her sign with a 'blue lives matter' flag.
Some counter protestors suggested, instead of repealing HALT, that the disgruntled officers get another job, and one claimed, 'They're only out here because they're being held accountable for murder.'
