title: Governor Lights State Landmarks, Expands Health Services on Women's Equality Day
author: JANANI HARIRAM
description: On Women's Equality Day, Gov. Kathy Hochul signed a bill that provides insurance coverage for tattooing as a part of breast reconstruction surgery and another that requires menstrual products to be…
content:
Photo by Darren McGee, courtesy of the Governor's Office
Landmarks across New York, including the SUNY Administration Building pictured here, are lit purple and gold on August 26 in honor of Women's Equality Day. Additionally, Gov. Kathy Hochul signed two bills to expand resources for women's health services.
On Women's Equality Day, Gov. Kathy Hochul signed a bill that provides insurance coverage for tattooing as a part of breast reconstruction surgery and another that requires menstrual products to be available in public universities.
Bill S.6146-A/A.5729-A ensures that tattooing performed by a physician as part of breast reconstruction will be covered by commercial health providers. It passed the Senate floor with 61 votes for and none against. State Senator Cordell Cleare, the prime sponsor of the Senate bill, said, 'I want to thank Gov. Hochul for signing this very important bill, to help our survivors heal physically, mentally, and emotionally.'
Bill S.5910-B/A.4060-A provides menstrual products in all restrooms in SUNY and CUNY buildings. It passed the Senate with 57 votes for and 2 against. State Senator Michelle Hinchey, the Senate sponsor of the bill, said, 'This legislation is a huge step forward in our fight to end period poverty, reduce financial stress and stigma often surrounding menstruation.'
'Menstrual products provided in campus bathrooms have actually benefited me a lot, and it's plainly obvious how this can be beneficial to other people, too,' said a SUNY New Paltz student who asked to remain anonymous. 'On the days where I'm in a rush in the morning and I forget to pack a couple of pads for myself, I can at least know that I have one to change into when I'm on the go.'
Both bills were championed in the Assembly by Amy Paulin, the chair of the Assembly Health Committee.
'I think [the legislation] will help address needs that vulnerable, poor young women have when they have to choose between taking care of this health need and other important things they have to pay for,' Paulin said.
Hochul is the first female governor of New York and says in her press release, 'New York will always be a leader in protecting and expanding women's rights.'
With women's health and reproductive rights being a major topic of conversation in political and personal spaces, Hochul stands firm on her support for the reproductive freedom and the bodily autonomy of women. Politico writes, 'She's directed millions in state funds to abortion providers. She's made sure out-of-staters can get abortion pills from New York doctors without concern for retaliation.'
Hochul has stated that she will run for reelection in 2026, and one can expect women's rights and abortion issues to be major arguments in her campaign given her current trajectory.
Hochul has officially declared August 26 Women's Equality Day in New York State and writes in her declaration, 'our nation continues to contend with the immense setback caused by the June 24 2022 Supreme Court decision to end U.S Constitutional protection for abortion rights; as long as I am governor, New York State will protect women's rights.'
Women's Equality Day was first recognized by Congress in 1973 and commemorates the adoption of the 19th amendment by the United States, granting women the right to vote
To commemorate the day, landmarks across the state were lit purple and gold throughout the state, including the Albany International Airport Gateway and the H. Carl McCall SUNY Building.

title: New Law Requires Gambling Addiction Warnings on Every Gaming and Wagering Ad in New York
author: RYAN CARRION
description: A new law taking effect December 1 will require warnings about problem gambling on every gambling and sports betting advertisement in the state of New York. Gov. Kathy Hochul signed legislation…
content:
Photo courtesy of the New York State Office of Addiction Services and Supports.
A new law taking effect December 1 will require warnings about problem gambling on every gambling and sports betting advertisement in the state of New York.
Gov. Kathy Hochul signed legislation S.1550 / A.1118 on October 1, requiring all advertisements for gambling and sports betting to include warnings about the potential harm and addictive effects of gambling. A gambling hotline number must be posted clearly and conspicuously with each advertisement and this new legislation adds on to clarify that mobile sports wagering advertisements are subjected to the same conditions that apply to other gaming-related advertisements.
'New York residents have access to various gambling options, including casinos, racetracks, the lottery and sports betting platforms like FanDuel and DraftKings,' said Sen. Leroy Comrie, the bill's prime sponsor. 'It's essential that users are informed about the risks of addiction and know where to seek help if needed. While revenue for the state is certainly important, promoting responsible gambling and safeguarding our communities is also critical.'
As the football season approaches playoff season and the SuperBowl, and the NBA and NHL seasons get into full swing, gambling remains a huge part of professional sports, but can also create a 'hidden addiction' in many, since there are often no outward physical signs.
Financial, emotional, social, occupational, and physical harm with devastating consequences for individuals, as well as their families and friends, are just a few of the many negatives of this severe addiction that ruins lives.
'More people than ever are able to access gambling, so as these opportunities increase, it is important that we continue our efforts to educate New Yorkers about the risks associated with problem gambling and where they can find help and support,' said Chinazo Cunningham, the commissioner of New York State Office of Addiction Services and Supports.
Those seeking help for their gambling problem have an increasing number of options to find help in New York state, including inpatient, outpatient, residential programs and recovery support systems, through highly skilled and educated professional certified providers, State-operated treatment services, and a strong private practitioner network. Regional problem gambling resource centers, which are funded by the Office of Addiction Services and Supports and operated by the New York Council on Problem Gambling , can provide resources including information, training, and connections to help. These centers are available in every part of the state.
'Protecting New Yorkers from the dangerous and addictive effects of problem gambling and sports betting is vitally important for the prosperity of our great state,' Gov. Hochul said. 'I want New Yorkers to be able to safely enjoy the activities they love, while proceeding with caution when necessary.'
According to the bill's justification, ' As gambling becomes more easily accessed by more people, the number of lives negatively affected by gambling has also increased. This can lead to serious consequences for both the gambler and their family.'
New York State Gaming Commission Chair Brian O'Dwyer said, 'New York state recognizes the importance of responsible gaming practices and has strong safeguards in place to protect and educate bettors. While the Gaming Commission already requires sports wagering operators to include problem gambling messaging on all advertisements, we are encouraged that this common-sense measure has been codified into state law. By signing this bill, Governor Hochul continues to deliver smart and responsible gaming policies that help support our state.'
The bill's justification goes on to state, the National Council on Problem Gambling defines problem gambling as, gambling behavior which causes disruptions in any major area of life: psychological, physical, social or vocational. This may include pathological and compulsive gambling, which is a form of addiction that grows worse as time progresses. Statistics show that approximately 2.6 percent of the U.S. population has some type of gambling issue. That adds up to nearly 10 million people in the United States who struggle with a gambling habit.
'These new changes to the gambling advertisements law will help to promote responsible gaming practices and provide support for those who need it,' said Clyde Vanel, sponsor of the Assembly bill.

title: Stefanik Gets High Praise From New York Republicans As She Prepares For New UN Role
author: Janani Hariram
description: New York's 21st District Congresswoman and House Republican Conference Chair Elise Stefanik has been called to serve in President Trump's Cabinet as U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations. Stefanik was the youngest woman ever elected to Congress and became the most senior woman in House Republican leadership. According to The […]
content:
New York's 21st District Congresswoman and House Republican Conference Chair Elise Stefanik has been called to serve in President Trump's Cabinet as U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations.
Stefanik was the youngest woman ever elected to Congress and became the most senior woman in House Republican leadership. According to The New York Times, 'Her foreign policy views track with Mr. Trump's. A staunch supporter of Israel, she has repeatedly accused the U.N. of being plagued by 'antisemitic rot' and proposed blocking funding for the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees.'
In her new role, Stefanik will represent the United States on the UN Security Council, and during meetings of the General Assembly.
'The work ahead is immense as we see antisemitism skyrocketing coupled with four years of catastrophically weak U.S. leadership that significantly weakened our national security and diminished our standing in the eyes of both allies and adversaries,' Stefanik said in a statement following her nomination. 'I stand ready to advance President Donald Trump's restoration of America First, peace-through-strength leadership on the world stage on day one at the United Nations.
'No matter where this journey takes us, upstate New York — the cradle of the American Revolution — will always be my heart and home.'
Her nomination has been met with approval from a majority of the Republican Party. New York Republican Committee Chair Ed Cox said, 'as ambassador, Elise will bring her deep understanding of complex international issues, her commitment to a strong national defense, and her clear-eyed vision of American sovereignty and strength.'
New York State Conservative Party Chairman Gerard Kassar said in his statement, 'Congresswoman Stefanik is smart, savvy, and fearless in the face of adversity. She will represent American interests at the world body with a tenacity unseen in years.'
In the hours and days after her nomination, several of Stefanik's Republican colleagues in the House voiced their support, including Nick Langworthy, Anthony D'Esposito, Marc Molinaro, Mike Lawler and Nicole Malliotakis.
'Elise was a fantastic conference chair and she'll be a great ambassador,' Malliotakis said. 'Looking forward to working with her in her new role based here in New York City.'
President Trump touts her credentials in his statement, 'Elise is a strong and very smart America First fighter. She graduated from Harvard University, with honors, was the youngest woman ever elected to Congress, and is the highest ranking woman in Congress, as the House Republican Conference Chair. She was the first Member of Congress to endorse me, and has always been a staunch advocate.'
However, John Bolton, a former U.S. national security adviser under Trump and ambassador to the U.N. during the Bush administration, told The Associated Press, 'She wants to run for president in 2028. She realizes she has no foreign policy experience so what better way than to become U.N. ambassador. She stays two years, and then away we go.'
Stefanik started publicly endorsing and supporting Trump when Democrats planned to impeach him in 2019, defending him staunchly in the committee hearings and continuing her backing in the following years. She backed his claims about the 2020 election being stolen and endorsed him in the 2024 election before he announced his intention to run for the White House.
Steve Peoples of the Associated Press wrote, 'Stefanik's evolution is the story of the modern Republican Party, which has come to believe that the path to power and fundraising success runs through Trump, whether party members like him or not.'
According to the BBC, 'she argued there should be a 'complete reassessment of US funding of the United Nations' after the Palestinian Authority tried to expel Israel from the UN over human rights abuses in Gaza.' She seems to intend to make many changes to the UN budget that fall in line with Trumpian politics, the effects of which we shall soon see.
Stefanik is required to give up her House seat to ascend to the UN, so the Democrats and the Republicans will both be looking to take her North Country seat as they continue to fight for control of the House. Gov. Kathy Hochul will be required to call a special election in the 21st Congressional District once Stefanik officially resigns from Congress.
Elon Musk, billionaire Trump supporter, said on his social media platform X, 'Elise is awesome, but it might be too dicey to lose her from the House, at least for now.'

title: Hochul Prioritizes Family Affordability in State of the State Address
author: KYLE BREDBERG
description: Children and middle-class families were the emphasis of Gov. Hochul's recent State of the State Address, in which she outlined her plans to lower the cost of living for New York households. Hochul…
content:
Photo by Mike Groll, courtesy of the Governor's Office
Children and middle-class families were the emphasis of Gov. Hochul's recent State of the State Address, in which she outlined her plans to lower the cost of living for New York households.
Hochul outlined a range of proposals relating to middle class families and childcare, sharing her plans for tax cuts, expanding the child tax credit, implementing universal school lunch, and stating her desire for universal childcare.
'Your family is my fight,' Hochul said near the beginning of her confident, 54-minute speech. 'I will never stop finding ways to put money in your pocket.'
Hochul delivered her fourth State of the State Address in the Hart Theater of the Egg Performing Arts Center in Albany on January 14 to a full house of lawmakers, union leaders, clergy, county executives, district attorneys and other elected officials.
Her top priority was affordability, with public safety, mental health and infrastructure improvements also being emphasized. Hochul also touched on housing, proposing a law preventing private equity companies from bidding on a property until it has been on the market for 75 days, receiving emphatic applause. She outlined all her proposals for the upcoming year in her 2025 State of the State book.
The first of the governor's plans to increase affordability is through what she calls a 'sweeping middle class tax cut,' a tax cut of up to 5 percent for New York households making less than $323,000 a year. According to Hochul, this will provide more than $1 billion collectively in tax relief to families statewide.
'The tax cuts I propose today, and will fight for in the coming months, will deliver the lowest tax rates in 70 years,' Hochul said.
If passed, these cuts which affect five of New York's nine tax brackets, will come into effect during the 2025 tax season and impact 8.3 million residents. 'By itself, it's a monumental win for New Yorkers in the battle for affordability,' the governor said.
Following this announcement, Hochul proposed an inflation refund, a plan to distribute $3 billion of surplus sales tax revenue to qualifying New Yorkers. 'Because prices went up, our sales tax revenue went up as well,' Hochul said. 'That extra money does not belong in state coffers. It belongs back in your pocket.'
Individuals making less than $150,000, and families making under $300,000, are eligible for the rebate and will receive a single, direct payment of either $300, for individual filers, or $500 for joint filers. These payments will go to 8.6 million New Yorkers.
Additionally, the governor announced her two-year plan to expand the child tax credit.
Currently, a family with a child under four is eligible for a maximum credit of $330. Under this new proposal, that maximum credit would be increased to $1,000.
The governor hopes to expand the program even more, increasing the credit for children aged 4 to 16, to $500 in 2026.
'It makes good economic sense,' Hochul said. 'Every dollar invested into the child tax credit will generate one dollar and 25 cents in economic activity.' Photo by Darren McGee, courtesy of the Governor's Office
Hochul also plans to implement free breakfast and lunch at all the state's schools, saving parents $165 a month in groceries and improving student performance and quality of life.
According to Hochul, it is unacceptable that many students are consistently going to school hungry. 'In the wealthiest nation in the world, this can no longer be tolerated. Not in America, and definitely not in the great state of New York.'
According to the governor, these four proposals could provide qualifying New Yorker families with nearly $5,000 in savings this coming year.
The cost of childcare was also something Hochul emphasized, comparing the cost to a second rent payment. 'If you're making minimum wage, it doesn't add up,' Hochul said. 'When my kids were young, I had to leave my job because I couldn't find accessible, affordable childcare.'
Hochul then called on the Legislature to partner with her to put the state on a pathway to universal childcare. To do this, Hochul plans to create the New York Coalition for Child Care with the aim of finding a sustainable, equitable route to universal childcare.
'In the meantime, we're going to dedicate $110 million dollars to build new childcare centers, renovate existing ones, and expand options for families and communities all over New York,' Hochul said.
In addition to this, Hochul hopes to create a pool of substitute childcare workers, able to be hired as needed, to prevent childcare facilities from shutting down because of an unexpected staffing shortage.
Hochul also launched the Unplug and Play initiative, a program that aims to steer kids away from social media, by providing them with alternative recreational activities. 'We must give them safe places to simply be kids. It's just common sense,' Hochul said.
The initiative includes a commitment to invest in New York social infrastructure, such as playgrounds and pools, and the launching of NY BRICKS, a program that would provide grants to nonprofits for community center projects.
'We'll build new playgrounds, we'll create hundreds of new opportunities for kids to join music and drama clubs, join youth volunteer organizations, sports teams,' Hochul said. 'These activities are transformative.'
With these, Hochul will launch Get Offline Get Outside 2.0, a commitment to increasing funding to youth programming and sports teams that will lead to an additional 100,000 open slots in these programs.
'That's our 2025 blueprint as we continue the fight for New York's children and families,' Hochul said. Watch the governor's full State of the State Address below:

title: Kavanagh, Kelles Introduce Food Safety and Chemical Disclosure Act
author: MIA QUICK
description: The Food Safety and Chemical Disclosure Act, sponsored by Sen. Brian Kavanagh and Assemblymember Dr. Anna Kelles, attempts to close loopholes in the Food and Drug Administration's regulation of…
content:
Photo courtesy of Sen. Brian Kavanagh's Office
Sen. Brian Kavanagh, at podium, and Assembly Member Anna Kelles, right, unveil their Food Safety and Chemical Disclosure Act at the State Capitol on February 4. They were joined by a coalition that wants to increase public awareness about harmful food additives and close reporting loopholes for some ingredients that can be added in secret by food producers.
The Food Safety and Chemical Disclosure Act, sponsored by Sen. Brian Kavanagh and Assemblymember Dr. Anna Kelles, attempts to close loopholes in the Food and Drug Administration's regulation of substances classified as 'generally recognized as safe.' A coalition in support of the bill ( S.1239 / A.1556 ) made their voices heard during a rally in the State Capitol on February 4.
The legislation would ban food additives, synthetic dyes, and certain chemicals that are manufactured in New York state and distributed in schools. The act would ban Red No. 3, potassium bromate, and propylparabens. It would prohibit the sale of synthetic food dyes sold in schools such as Red 3, Red 40, Blue 1, Blue 2, Green 3, Yellow 5, and Yellow 6. This would ensure transparency of ingredients used by companies and the process of determining what is 'generally regarded as safe.' The data would be made publicly available through the New York State Department of Agriculture and Markets.
'New Yorkers need and deserve the highest level of protection when it comes to the safety of the food we eat,' said Kavanagh, D-Manhattan.
Toxic additives and synthetic dyes have been associated with causing cancer in animal studies, neurobehavioral issues and hyperactivity in children, and behavioral health and neurological issues. Potassium bromate and propylparabens are banned in the European Union and they have been replaced by substitute ingredients.
FDA has officially banned Red 3, with the phase out process planned on being completed by 2027.
'It took the FDA 35 years to ban Red 3. New York can't wait another 35 years to ban the other six dangerously synthetic dyes in our school foods,' said Sarah Sorscher, director of Regulatory Affairs at the Center of Science in the Public Interest.
The Food Safety and Chemical Disclosure Act attempts to directly combat the loophole in the GRAS rule, a requirement for companies to self-certify their food additives. Manufacturers are expected to enlist experts that are unbiased in their ruling of GRAS. When companies determine their products are safe for the general public, they can be sold.
A lawsuit filed against the FDA ruled, in 2021, that the FDA's GRAS rule is lawfully exercised. The FDA won't administer their own tests prior to allowing a company to release their product unless an ingredient is proven to cause harm to the general public.
This ruling is partially attributed to Congress' Food Additives Amendment of 1958, which did not make GRAS notifications to the FDA mandatory.
'Why would you be pushing back unless you have something to hide,' Kelles, D-Ithaca, asked in reference to the companies that oppose the act.
On Feb. 4, legislators and food safety advocates convened at the Capitol to announce a coalition to increase public awareness and garner support for the bill. The coalition included Consumer Reports, Environmental Working Group, Clean+Healthy, The Center for Science in the Public Interest, Muslim Community Network, and New York State Council of Churches.
The coalition wants to pass the legislation by next month as part of the state budget process. If passed, it would be enacted 180 days after becoming law and small businesses would have a three-year grace period.
Mia Quick is a contributing writer and videographer for The Legislative Gazette, studying journalism at SUNY New Paltz. She is interested in pursuing environmental and travel journalism during her career.

title: Bill Would Fast-Track New Housing Built On Religious Properties
author: MATT GARTON
description: Faith leaders, lawmakers and housing activists are supporting two new bills they say would mitigate the state's housing crisis while shoring up revenues for land-rich, cash-poor churches, temples,…
content:
Photo courtesy of the New York State Senate
Sen. Andrew Gounardes, at podium, is joined by faith leaders on March 5, 2024 to promote one of his bills that would make it easier for churches, synagogues, temples, mosques and other religious groups to build new housing on their land. The bill has been reintroduced this session, with Brian Cunningham sponsoring it in the Assembly.
Faith leaders, lawmakers and housing activists are supporting two new bills they say would mitigate the state's housing crisis while shoring up revenues for land-rich, cash-poor churches, temples, synagogues and mosques.
The New York Faith Based Housing Coalition held a rally on the Million Dollar Staircase on February 4, launching their new 2025 campaign to address the ongoing housing and affordability crisis. The legislation at center-stage is the Faith-Based Affordable Housing Act ( S.3397 / A.3647 ), which aims to create more than 60,000 new homes on surplus land owned by faith institutions.
According to the bill's justification, the legislation would 'dramatically' accelerate the timeline on which affordable housing on religious property can be built while reducing bureaucratic hurdles.
It would allow houses of worship such as temples, synagogues, mosques, and churches to bypass local zoning rules as long as they are building affordable housing that complies with 'reasonable' density standards: 30 units per acre for small municipalities with less than 50,000 people and 50 units per acre for localities with more than 50,000 people.
'The Faith-Based Affordable Housing Act will enable faith leaders to further serve their communities by creating desperately needed affordable housing,' said Xellex Rivera, the chief program officer at Housing Solutions of New York.
According to NYU's Furman Center , religious organizations in New York City own 86 million square feet of permitted residential land. If this land were used to its fullest capacity without barriers, it would result in an estimated 98,000 homes in multi-family buildings.
Faith leaders, like Rev. Dustin Longmire of Messiah Lutheran Church in Rotterdam, Schenectady County, have witnessed the housing affordability crisis firsthand.
'I've seen members of our congregation become homeless because there was nothing they could afford. We need faith housing here in Rotterdam, and we're calling on the State Legislature to help let us build it,' said Longmire.
The Faith-Based Affordable Housing Act is sponsored by Senator Andrew Gounardes and Assembly Member Brian Cunningham, along with 58 co-sponsors in the Senate and Assembly.
'As legislators, we must use every legal tool at our disposal to ensure no one is denied a home,' Cunningham said. 'We have to pass The Faith-Based Affordable Housing Act to bring us closer to ending the housing crisis — one that has persisted for far too long.'
This effort would be financially supported by pre-development grant funding with no cost to local governments or taxpayers.
'Across the state, families are struggling to make ends meet, and when they can't afford to pay skyrocketing housing costs, they leave,' said Gournardes. 'My Faith-Based Affordable Housing Act allows trusted houses of worship to more easily build affordable housing on land they already own, creating new homes for tens of thousands of New Yorkers.'
The Housing Access Voucher Program ( S.568B / A.1704 ), also referred to as HAVP, is a bill sponsored by Senate Housing Chair Brian Kavanagh and Assembly Housing Chair Linda Rosenthal. It would set up a statewide rental subsidy program for low-income families and individuals who face housing loss and eviction.
'In this state, we need to provide vouchers for people so they can stay in their apartments and also escape homelessness,' Rosenthal said. 'People in this state are increasingly finding that they can't afford to stay here anymore, and that ain't right.'
This program seeks to help tenants remain in permanent housing. If tenants are able to contribute 30% of their income towards rent, HAVP will cover the rest.
Both bills remain in their respective Senate and Assembly committees.

title: After Weeks Of Strikes, Corrections Officers Make Presence Known At State Capitol
author: THE LEGISLATIVE GAZETTE
description: Hundreds of corrections officers from across New York rallied outside the state Capitol Tuesday amid an ongoing strike over working conditions in state prisons. The corrections officers, their family…
content:
Legislative Gazette photo by Nicholas Guercio. Cover photo by Mia Quick.
Hundreds of corrections officers from across New York rallied outside the state Capitol Tuesday amid an ongoing strike over working conditions in state prisons.
The corrections officers, their family members and allied lawmakers demanded better working conditions inside state prisons and a legislative repeal of the HALT Act, a 2022 law that limits the use of solitary confinement for prisoners.
'Two things need to happen, the HALT Act must be repealed and Kathy Hochul must resign,' said Steve McLaughlin, the Rensselaer County executive who joined other lawmakers and elected officials addressing the protesters.
Michael Sussman, a civil rights attorney and candidate for Orange County executive, was the leader of the protest despite his affiliation with the Democratic Party. 'Polarization is not to accomplish anything. It will allow you to be marginalized, which is what's happened so far. We have to fight strongly against that, and that's why I'm here,' said Sussman.
'The last place most people who know me would think I'm going to be here, but they're wrong.'
He was joined at Tuesday's rally by Sen. Dan Stec, R-Queensbury, Assemblyman Brian Maher, R-Walden, Sen. Mario Mattera, R-St. James, and Sen. Mark Walczyk, R-Watertown. The politicians came in support of the protesters, demanding that immediate change needs to happen.
Currently, there is a bill ( S.2656/A.3217 ) sponsored by Sen. Dan Stec, R-Queensbury, and Assemblyman Matt Simpson, R-Lake George which would answer some of the protestors' concerns to repeal the HALT Act.
The bill states that this act 'has severely restricted the ability to use segregated confinement for prisoners that break the rules and engage in violent behavior.'
Even though the repealer bill was first proposed in 2022 — the year the HALT Act was implemented — protesters in support of the correctional officers hope recent scrutiny of the state prison system will help it advance. Some were family members of correction officers who shared their personal concerns with the current working conditions. They spoke about their loved ones' safety and the long hours they work, often forced to work double shifts with little warning.
'Us kids deserve to have parents that come home,' said the daughter of a correction officer who often received mandated overtime.
Anthony Bernard, a retired corrections officer, explained how some workers 'get stuck with 24 to 32 hours straight' shifts.
'Biggest thing is we're not safe,' said an anonymous protester. 'We already work in an unsafe job. We know that, we expect that. But when the government puts legislation in place to make it even more unsafe, that's where we have a problem.' Legislative Gazette photo by Jamie Case
As the protest continued, a smaller group of counter protesters from Jails Justice Network, an organization that attempts to reform corrections policy, joined by others, stood a few feet away from the rally after attending their own event in the Capitol.
The held signs that read, 'brutality, rape, and murder are not in the job description,' 'incarcerated lives matter,' and 'Robert Brooks — say his name.' Brooks was an inmate who died a day after a beating he received from several corrections officers at Marcy Correctional Facility late last year. Body camera footage showed Brooks handcuffed and beaten in the facility.
The counter protesters sad they fear what could happen to incarcerated individuals if the HALT Act is repealed, they want a system that will protect prisoners just as much as the guards.
'I was handcuffed, shackled, and beaten,' said Thomas Kearney, formerly incarcerated and the co-organizer for NYS Jails Justice Network and former Prison Rape Elimination Act outreach director for the NYS Coalition Against Sexual Assault. 'After, I was charged with aggravated assault.'
'We're talking about a system that people should be putting love at,' said Rory Smalls, a member of NYS Jails Justice Network, 'They want certain things removed to do sneaky things.'
The corrections officers chanted Gov. Kathy Hochul's name as she was hosting an unrelated roundtable discussion about the impact of recent tariffs imposed by President Trump.
Hochul was asked for her thoughts on the ongoing prison strike, and the protest happening on the Capitol lawn below.
'There is no justification to break the law in the state of New York, and they need to get back to work, because they have created a dangerous situation for the other correction officers who lived up to their duty and their oath and the law, and are in those environments,' Hochul said.
The governor said the 'screaming and yelling' would have 'no impact' on her.
Hochul said that while she has been actively engaging with corrections officers to hear their concerns, the strike in question is both illegal and unauthorized, citing the Taylor Law.
She emphasized that, due to NYSCOPBA's declaration of the strike's illegality from the outset, negotiations are complicated, as no one at the table can legally represent the workers involved.
'I know what I have to do, and I believe they should be getting back to work. There are serious consequences. We have warned them,' Hochul said.
Gazette staff writers Jamie Case, Matt Garton, Olivia Sippel and Mia Quick contributed to this article.

title: Gov. Hochul Embeds OGS Commissioner in Office of Cannabis Management For 'Top-Down Review'
description: Gov. Kathy Hochul today initiated an assessment of the Office of Cannabis Management to identify opportunities for improvement and begin implementation of a strategic plan for the long-term success of…
content:
Photo courtesy of the Governor's Office Gov. Kathy Hochul today initiated an assessment of the Office of Cannabis Management to identify opportunities for improvement and begin implementation of a strategic plan for the long-term success of the legal cannabis rollout. Commissioner for the Office of General Services Jeanette Moy will serve as lead and executive sponsor of the effort, supported by experienced state government leaders. Moy will embed in the Office of Cannabis Management for at least 30 days to assess the agency's organization. As part of the plan, several goals have been identified, including: Top-down review of organizational structure, processes, and systems with a focus on improving OCM license processing times and application-to-opening timeframes for new cannabis retailers and businesses.
Develop key performance metrics and an executive-level licensing dashboard to provide the Executive Chamber with a timely, accurate, and comprehensive picture of licensing activity for legal retailers.
Identify and implement changes to policy, procedure, and regulation — within the bounds of the Marihuana Regulation and Taxation Act — to streamline the licensing process and simplify application and review for prospective licensees.
Develop three-month and six-month action plans with organizational change initiatives, milestones, and actions to continue improving agency functions while developing a world-class licensing and regulatory agency for New York states' cannabis industry. 'Today, we take the first step in revamping New York's legal cannabis industry to ensure its long-term success,' Gov. Hochul said. 'I have full confidence in Commissioner Moy's ability to identify areas that need improvement, establish standards and processes across agencies, and jumpstart the next phase of New York's legal cannabis market. OGS Commissioner Jeannette Moy Moy will have access to resources from OGS, the Office of Information Technology Services, and other state agencies. Following the initial 30-day period, the potential for external consulting may be considered to support a second, longer-duration phase of the effort. Gov. Hochul and others have been critical of the rollout of New York's adult-use cannabis marketplace in recent months, pointing to delays in handing out retail licenses, confusion among consumers, and frustration on the part of growers. 'We have built a cannabis market based on equity, and there is a lot to be proud of,' New York State Office of Cannabis Management Executive Direct Chris Alexander said. 'At the same time, there is more we can do to improve OCM's operations. 'We owe it to operators across the supply chain and consumers alike, who are looking for more access and opportunity in our budding, regulated market,' Alexander added. 'At the end of the day, it's all about doing what's right for New Yorkers.'

title: Fair Elections Coalition Applauds $114.5M Budget Agreement for New Public Campaign Finance Program
description: A coalition of good-government groups is applauding the Senate and Assembly for including $114.5 million for the New York State Public Campaign Finance Program in their one-house budget bills,…
content: Legislative Gazette file photos A coalition of good-government groups is applauding the Senate and Assembly for including $114.5 million for the New York State Public Campaign Finance Program in their one-house budget bills, matching the governor's budget allocation. The funds would cover $14.5 million in administrative costs and $100 million for public matching funds for qualified candidates. Only individual small donations qualify for matching and there's a maximum for how much they can claim. The Fair Elections for NY coalition issued a statement in response. 'New York state is now poised to become the largest state in the country to have public campaign financing in place for a state election cycle,' the statement reads. 'This program is nothing short of transformational. It will bring more everyday New Yorkers into the political process, both as donors and candidates.' 'It will counter the toxic influence of big money on our elections and government. And it will serve as a shining example for the nation. More than 300 candidates are registered with the Public Campaign Finance Board for the 2024 election, including incumbents and challengers, Democrats and Republicans from across the state. We eagerly await the passage and signage of the full state budget.' The Executive and Assembly budgets each propose $114.5 million for the campaign matching funds and the Senate budget proposes $194.5 million for the program, which already has 300 candidates signed up. 'The Public Campaign Finance Program promises to make everyday donors a far more important part of the political process,' said Joanna Zdanys, senior counsel-manager at the Brennan Center for Justice during testimony before the Legislature last month. 'In the 2022 state elections, small donors were responsible for only 11 percent of giving to state legislative campaigns. Our data analyses show that if the program had been available that cycle, it could have increased small donor's fundraising share six-fold, from 11 percent to 67 percent.'

title: Kidnapping Case Highlights Need for Security Cameras at Park Entrances and Exits
author: Mariah Parmeter
description:
This week, Craig Ross Jr. will receive sentencing for kidnapping and sexually assaulting a 9-year old girl from Moreau State Park in Saratoga County last fall. Ross faces 47 years to life in prison after pleading guilty back in February.
Senator Jim Tedisco, R-Ballston Lake, and Assemblyman Ange
content:
This week, Craig Ross Jr. will receive sentencing for kidnapping and sexually assaulting a 9-year old girl from Moreau State Park in Saratoga County last fall. Ross faces 47 years to life in prison after pleading guilty back in February.
Senator Jim Tedisco, R-Ballston Lake, and Assemblyman Angelo Santabarbara, D-Rotterdam, are currently sponsoring legislation (S.7688/A.8141) that would require the installation of security camera systems that would allow for the identification of make, model, and plate number of vehicles entering and exiting any state park, historic site, campground, or recreational facilities.
This case made national news and inspired Tedisco and Santabarbara to draft the legislation within days of the case. 'If we had those cameras, he had a car, we could have gotten his license plate' said Tedisco. This type of surveillance would be an important tool to aid law enforcement in the future, the lawmakers say.
The girl disappeared on September 30, 2023 after going for a bike ride at Moreau Lake State Park. She had been riding with friends and decided to go on one last ride alone, and wasn't seen again for two days. She was found hidden in a cabinet inside a trailer found behind Ross's mothers house. Ross was found after the girl's family received a ransom note that had his fingerprints on it.
Senator Tedisco has sponsored several bills and initiatives in his career that helps families of missing persons, he is known within the state Legislature as an expert on the subject. He continuously joins Mary Lyall, a Ballston Spa resident, and the Center for Hope at their annual New York State Missing Persons Day Ceremony.
Missing Persons Day is organized by Mary Lyall, who started The Center for Hope along with her late husband. The Center for Hope is a nonprofit organization whose mission is to provide resources to educate, assist, and support families and friends in coping with unexplained disappearances. This organization should 'enhance the ability to find these people,' said Tedisco.
Lyall and her husband started The Center for Hope after their daughter, Suzanne G. Lyall went missing. On March 2, 1998 the undergraduate student at SUNY Albany left her job at the Babbage's in Crossgates mall, after the store closed, and has not been seen since. She was believed to have taken a city bus from the mall back to campus, where a friend claims she saw her get off the bus at Collins Circle, however, it has not been confirmed.
There were a couple suspects including her boyfriend at the time, who hasn't been able to be completely ruled out as a suspect. There was also a man who used the ATM around the same time Lyall's credit card was reportedly used. But no usable security footage was uncovered, and he has since been ruled out.
Disappearances and abductions are too common in the United States, especially in and around state parks. The proposed legislation (S.7688/A.8141) would be a practical step to help stop abductions, Tedisco said. He added that another important step is education, not only in schools, but for parents, 'not to freak out the kids,' but to teach them the signs of stranger-danger, explained Tedisco.
The governor has included funding for security cameras at park entrances and exits in her proposed state budget.

title: Zeldin Meeting With Key Lawmakers Ahead of Confirmation Proceedings
author: RYAN CARRION
description: Lee Zeldin — Donald Trump's pick for EPA administrator — met with a key U.S. senator this week who will play an important role in helping him through the confirmation process and onto the president's…
content: Iran plans a major increase in the production rate of highly enriched uranium, the UN nuclear watchdog said Friday in a confidential report seen by AFP. An updated design of Iran's Fordo plant showed that the effect of the change "would be to significantly increase the rate of production of uranium enriched up to 60 percent", the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) report said. Production will jump to more than 34 kilogrammes of highly enriched uranium per month, compared to 4.7 kilogrammes previously, added the report to the IAEA's board of governors. Uranium enriched to 60 percent brings it closer to the 90 percent needed to make a nuclear weapon. Iran denies it wants nuclear arms. Speaking to AFP in Bahrain, IAEA chief Rafael Grossi said Iran was sending a "clear message" after it was recently censured by the nuclear body's board of governors. "This is a clear message that they are responding to what they feel is pressure," Grossi said on the sidelines of the Manama Dialogue conference. Last month, Iran said it would launch "new and advanced" centrifuges in response to an IAEA resolution that censured Tehran for what the agency called lack of cooperation. The censure motion brought by Britain, France, Germany, and the United States at the IAEA's 35-nation board follows a similar one in June. "Quite clearly what has happened is in response to this, this is very clear," Grossi said, adding: "The significance cannot be underestimated." In its report, the IAEA called on Iran to implement stepped-up inspections by the agency "as a matter of urgency". Those will "enable the agency to provide timely and technically credible assurances that the facility is not being misused to produce uranium of an enrichment level higher than that declared by Iran, and that there is no diversion of declared nuclear material," it added. Iran insists on its right to nuclear energy for peaceful purposes and has consistently denied any ambition of developing weapons capability. But according to the IAEA, it is the only non-nuclear-weapon state enriching uranium to 60 percent purity. A landmark 2015 nuclear deal between Tehran and major powers aimed to give Iran relief from crippling Western sanctions in exchange for limiting its nuclear programme to prevent it from developing weapons capability. Tehran kept to the accord, but in 2018, during Donald Trump's first US presidency, Washington unilaterally pulled out of the agreement and slapped heavy sanctions back on Iran, leading to the Islamic republic to step up its nuclear programme. Trump returns to office in January. Iran, Britain, France and Germany last week agreed at a meeting in Geneva to continue diplomatic talks. The meeting came amid surging tensions even before Trump's return to the White House. anb-jza/th/tw

title: Chief Judge Supports Bill That Gives "Second Look" at Long Prison Sentences
author: OLIVIA SHULTS
description: The chief judge of New York State's highest court, Rowan Wilson, presented his annual State of the Judiciary address at the Court of Appeals in Albany on Monday, February 10. During his address,…
content:
Legislative Gazette file photo
The chief judge of New York State's highest court, Rowan Wilson, presented his annual State of the Judiciary address at the Court of Appeals in Albany on Monday, February 10.
During his address, Wilson urged the Legislature to pass a bill that would allow incarcerated individuals to apply for reduced sentencing, to have a second chance at life outside the bars.
The proposed legislation, known as the Second Look Act, would authorize certain incarcerated individuals serving long sentences under the Department of Corrections and Community Supervision to apply for a sentence reduction. This would provide an opportunity for those serving ten years or more to request judges to reevaluate their sentences.
Although this legislation has been introduced in previous sessions ( S.321 / A.531 ), there is a new hope this year. Sponsors of the bill, Senator Julia Salazar, D-Brooklyn, and Assemblymember Latrice Walker, D-Brooklyn, support this legislation and Judge Wilson in his attempts to change the judiciary system.
In his opening remarks, Wilson said 'All of New York's courts should consider themselves problem solvers,' urging those who serve from the bench to ask 'what decision is best, not merely which party is right.' Chief Judge Rowan Wilson
Referring to the state's unified court system, Wilson said 'together we can provide better results for all New Yorkers… to bring our courts out of the past and into the future.'
Wilson noted that the United States is a world leader in incarceration per capita and that nearly half of those incarcerated in state prisons and jails have struggled with their mental health .
He builds his case further by acknowledging that 'our penal system is ill-equipped to provide mental health services to incarcerated people, and incarceration itself most often exacerbates existing or creates new mental health issues,' demonstrating concern over the correlation between inadequate mental health care and crime.
Last year's theme of enhanced diversion continues to be worked towards, with the Unified Court System and legislators working to expand diversion and treatment programs for people with mental health disorders and other disabilities.
Posing the question 'What do we get from all this incarceration?' Wilson acknowledged that incarceration doesn't make us any safer and studies prove that as our prison population increases, so does the crime rate. Backing this, he drew attention to the fact that The United States has one of the highest recidivism rates worldwide.
He continued on to mention the tremendous costs associated with a high level of incarceration, stating 'the annual cost per incarcerated person, in 2021, was well over half a million dollars.'
The monetary cost of incarceration does not convey the associated vast social and economic costs that disproportionately affect low-income communities. These include the disruption of families and communities; the multitude of barriers for employment and education; a reduction in lifetime earnings; the permanent loss of voting rights; and the stigmas attached to criminal conviction.
'Put simply, our criminal justice system isn't working. Maybe it hasn't really ever worked,' said Wilson. He stated that our current criminal justice system entrenches poverty, perpetuates cycles of violence, and continues to harm many of the New Yorkers the justice system aims to protect and serve.
Continuing, he made it clear that over incarceration has everything to do with the courts. Wilson called attention to the courts' responsibility stating 'separation of powers does not mean that the three branches of government cannot work together to better society…everyone sentenced to a New York prison was sentenced by a judge of the Unified Court System.'
While last year's theme of enhanced diversion continues to be worked towards, in pursuit of this year's theme, legislators and the Unified Court System 'are working to refine legislation colloquially called the Second Look Act… which would allow those serving long prison sentences to demonstrate to a judge that their continued incarceration is no longer justified,' as stated by Wilson.
This piece of legislation is believed by Wilson to fundamentally embody the problem-solving ethos attempting to be instilled deeply in the state courts, proposing human-centric, community-oriented solutions that have the potential to reduce crime and save taxpayer dollars.
The goals outlined are to enhance public safety by focusing on rehabilitation to reduce incarceration, enhance the prospect for social integration, and decrease recidivism.
Commissioner of the Department of Corrections and Community Supervision, Daniel Martuscello, built on Hon. Wilson's stance advocating for a cultural transformation, focused on accountability, transparency, and integrity, within the judiciary and the Department of Corrections and Community Supervision.
Martuscello said, 'we can begin to change the narrative so that those impacted by the criminal justice system may be defined by the person they are today and the totality of their experiences, rather than the worst mistake of their lives.'
Speaking in support of the Second Look Act, Martuscello called attention to those incarcerated that do 'extraordinary things to transform themselves and their peers every day.' He mentioned those obtaining their GED, receiving certification in a vocational trade, mentoring, or achieving a college degree. One of the many people who spoke at the address, Christopher Martinez, a father, husband and convicted criminal, urged those listening to 'pause for a moment and consider Lady Justice.' He continued, 'She holds both a sword and the scales of justice… we can refine how Lady Justice uses her sword.' He also mentioned New York's motto 'Excelsior – ever upward' as a symbol of what the judiciary department should aim to live up to.
Wilson said the effects of incarceration go far beyond just the incarcerated individual, asking 'can we disregard the effect of Mr. Martinez's lifetime incarceration on his children? What is the right outcome now?'
Sean Pica, the president of Hudson Link for Higher Education, spoke at the address on the results of bringing associate and bachelor degree programs to men and women in prison.
He said 'the results are stunning… Our nearly 2,000 alumni have a recidivism rate of less than 2 percent, compared to an estimated 68 percent across the country.'
The program provides education to those in prisons for less than $5,000 per student per year, which is significantly less than the cost of incarcerating an individual in New York state.
Pica introduced Mujahideen Muhammad, a Hudson Link graduate, a leader, a mentor, and an individual who has spent two-thirds of his life incarcerated. Muhammad spoke on his experiences at Harlem Valley Juvenile Residential Facility, on Rikers Island, and at Sing Sing Correctional Facility. Mentioning the guidance that Hudson Link provided, Muhammad graduated with his Master's degree in professional studies with a 4.0 grade point average, while still incarcerated, providing a new found hope for himself and others.
He stated 'my education prepared me for release in a way I hadn't anticipated: it connected me to a community of support.' He now works at Columbia University, an Ivy League school, after being convicted of an A-1 felony. He is proof that there is hope for individuals seeking a second chance.
In addition to Hudson Link, there are a multitude of programs that work to convince young individuals in high crime-rate areas that there is more to life than crime, in addition to reintegrating convicted criminals into society. These programs include Project Restore Bed-Stuy , the New Beginnings initiative , and the Columbia Center for Justice .
The Second Look Act, building on these programs, would directly address the issue of lengthy sentences.
Jarrell Daniels, a community organizer and former inmate who is now earning a doctorate degree, spoke at the address, stating 'For many of us, our destiny seemed etched in stone: from poverty, to the precinct, to the courtroom, and ultimately to a prison cell. But now I know, that path is not immutable.'
In addition to Daniels, Tami Eldridge, a currently incarcerated woman at Bedford Hills Correctional Facility pursuing her second master's degree, spoke on the hope that education and choosing a worthy path provides. She quoted her favorite author, Viktor Frankl, 'Everything can be taken from a man but one thing: the last of human freedoms – to choose one's attitude in any given set of circumstances, to choose one's own way.'
In his closing remarks, Wilson talked about the hope this legislation can provide. 'Hope…for all those who are not the same person convicted of a terrible crime many years ago.' Closing the address with, 'What we are doing is not the best we can do… we can do better. Won't we?'

title: Extreme Risk Protection Orders Must Now Be Filed On Statewide Registry
author: MIA QUICK
description: A new provision of the state's "Red Flag Law" took effect on February 6, requiring broader notifications about those who may pose a danger to themselves or others. The Extreme Risk Protection Orders…
content:
Photo by Mike Groll, courtesy of the Governor's Office
On October 24, 2022, Governor Kathy Hochul announces a major expansion of the state's Red Flag Law at the State Capitol, following a racially motivated mass shooting in Buffalo in May 2022.
A new provision of the state's 'Red Flag Law' took effect on February 6, requiring broader notifications about those who may pose a danger to themselves or others.
The Extreme Risk Protection Orders are meant to prevents individuals who show signs of being a threat to themselves from possessing firearms, either temporarily or permanently, depending on the circumstances of their case.
A bill signed by Gov. Kathy Hochul in October 2024 ( S.3340 / A.5873 ) requires courts to notify the statewide registry of orders of protections and warrants when judges issue an Extreme Risk Protection Order. This safeguard ensures that ERPOs aren't overlooked and codifies what courts have already been doing in practice.
'Police officers can now quickly see if someone has an outstanding ERPO and better protect victims who face an ongoing risk of violence from someone in their life – and those who pose a risk to themselves,' said Senate bill sponsor Shelley Mayer, D-Yonkers.
The Assembly bill was sponsored by Charles Lavine, D-North Shore.
As of Feb. 3, 2025, approximately 14,000 temporary and permanent ERPOs have been ordered by courts statewide. This is 12 times more than before state laws took action after a racially motivated mass shooting in Buffalo, on May 14, 2022.
After the shooting, Hochul required all police departments to file for ERPOs when applicable. The list of people able to request an ERPO extended to include health care practitioners who have examined an individual within the last six months and required reports by mental health practitioners.
'By empowering law enforcement and judges to take action, we're getting guns off our streets and making our communities safer,' Hochul said in a press release.
Hochul hopes to continue the state's efforts against gun violence, as reflected in her FY26 Executive Budget, by funding police technology and equipment through a grant program and the Gun Involved Violence Elimination (GIVE) initiative, and proposes to create a mass violence crisis response team and increase the crime victim compensation cost of burial and funeral expenses.

title: Watchdogs Hope 2025 Is The Year FOIL Laws Get Fixed
author: LILLY SABELLA
description: Government accountability groups are asking the state Senate and Assembly to pass four bills to strengthen the state's Freedom of Information Law. The state's FOIL law allows citizens and journalists…
content:
Legislative Gazette file photo
Government accountability groups are asking the state Senate and Assembly to pass four bills to strengthen the state's Freedom of Information Law.
The state's FOIL law allows citizens and journalists to request access to public records kept by state agencies and local governments to increase transparency.
However, the freedom of information process can be long and full of setbacks. At times a request can leave someone waiting for months for a FOIL officer to process their request.
The four new bills are backed by groups such as the New York Coalition for Open Government and the Freedom of the Press Foundation. These groups seek to make the bureaucratic FOIL process clearer and easier to access.
'New York State's Freedom of Information Law is plagued by flaws, loopholes and easily misinterpreted language,' said Digital Forensics Director for The Legal Aid Society, Jerome Greco. 'The Legislature should pass this slate of bills to strengthen FOIL and take a significant step forward for government transparency.'
The Report Foil Activity Bill ( S.452 / A.2321 ) sponsored by Sen. Brad Hoylman-Sigal, D–Manhattan, would require agencies to report information about the number and nature of FOIL requests they get to the state Committee on Open Government. The Assembly version of the bill is sponsored by Assemblymember John McDonald, D–Cohoes. Even though it passed the last legislative session, the Senate failed to move it through committee.
Another bill concerns attorney fees involved in challenging a denied FOIL request. People may challenge a state agency by suing them in court if they believe the agency wrongfully rejected their request. If passed, the Strengthen FOIL Attorneys' Fees bill ( S.1418 / A.950 ) would reward a plaintiff's litigation fees upon successfully suing the agency, encouraging people to challenge denied FOIL requests. The bill is sponsored by Sen. John Liu, D–Flushing, and Assemblymember Phil Steck, D–Schenectady, in their respective houses. While this bill passed the Senate last session, it stalled in the Governmental Operations Assembly Committee.
The Limit Commercial FOIL Exemption Bill ( S.5000 / A.1410 ) suffered a similar fate last session with only its Senate version passing. It was first introduced to the legislature eight years ago by Sen. Hoylman-Sigal who is the current bill's sponsor, and the bill would expand public access to commercial records but has never moved beyond committee in the Assembly. Assemblymember Linda Rosenthal, D–Upper West Side, is the bill's current Assembly sponsor.
The government may exempt an entity's records from FOIL disclosure, and this exception is permanent. The bill would amend the exemption protocol by mandating the entity periodically to re-apply for exemption, rather than it being indefinite.
The fourth bill titled Reduce Agency FOIL Response Time ( S.2520 / A.3425 ) would reform the FOIL process by chipping away at the long processing times plaguing request filers. The bill reduces the amount of time agencies may take to respond to FOIL requests. Although the bill came close to being voted on the Senate floor, it ultimately failed passage in the Senate or Assembly. Assemblymember Steven Raga, D–Queens, has introduced the bill in the Assembly, with Sen. James Skoufis, D–Cornwall, sponsoring the Senate version.
'The Legislature has a big opportunity to transform FOIL in 2025, after coming so close last year,' said Legislative Director for Reinvent Albany Tom Speaker. 'Both the Senate and Assembly have shown clear interest in reform. It's time for them to work together.'

title: Hochul Wants Farmers To Arm Her With Data About Tariff Impacts In New York
author: JAMIE CASE
description: As new tariffs imposed by President Trump ripple through the economy, Gov. Kathy Hochul met with members of the New York Farm Bureau to discuss their fears moving forward. New York farmers say they…
content:
Legislative Gazette photo by Jamie Case
As new tariffs imposed by President Trump ripple through the economy, Gov. Kathy Hochul met with members of the New York Farm Bureau to discuss their fears moving forward. New York farmers say they are feeling the brunt of the impact, with shrinking profit margins, rising costs, and increasing uncertainty about the future of their businesses.
'These tariffs are going to have an impact on farmers in a place like New York, which is right on the border of Canada,' Hochul said. 'But this has a nationwide impact. They're anxious. They've got a lot of stress in their lives already. This is just one more layer they didn't need.'
In the Red Room of the State Capitol on Tuesday, Hochul met with members of the New York State Farm Bureau, state Agriculture Commissioner Richard Ball, and others, to discuss their concerns over retaliatory tariffs from Canada and Mexico, and how they might impact New York's $8.5 billion agricultural industry.
New York exports roughly 40 percent of its agricultural products to other countries, and retaliatory tariffs of up to 25 percent from Canada and China are putting those sales at risk. 'This is going to really hurt their margins,' Hochul said. 'It will make it more difficult for them, but also, the inputs coming into their farms, like potash — an essential fertilizer component — are getting more expensive.'
Increased costs are affecting the entire supply chain, from fertilizers to energy to packaging materials. Farmers who depend on Canada for wood shavings, used in livestock bedding, have already been notified of price hikes. Meanwhile, fears are growing that Washington state, the nation's top apple producer, could flood the domestic market if its usual exports to Mexico and other countries slow down. 'That's the fear I heard—that it will reduce the price of apples dramatically for our farmers and literally drive them out of business,' she said.
'U.S. dairy farmers exported nearly $9 billion globally in 2024, with the largest portion of these exports going to Canada, Mexico and China. While we support fair trade, our goal is always to provide affordable and accessible food for all New Yorkers while protecting our agricultural markets and lowering input costs for our farmers,' said New York Farm Bureau President, David Fisher.
New York is home to 32,000 family farms, and industry leaders worry that number is in danger of declining. 'That number should be increasing, not decreasing,' Gov. Hochul said. 'We have fifth-generation farmers at the table, but they're questioning whether they can pass their businesses on to their children in light of these stresses.'
The Trump Administration has placed a 25 percent tariff on all goods from Canada and Mexico as well as a 10 percent tariff on energy resources from Canada. The impact is expected to raise costs for the average New Yorker by as much as $1,200 a year
Politically, the impact of the tariffs has heightened tensions between state and federal leaders. 'I'm not in Washington. I'm not deciding that there should be a punitive tariff that's going to affect every single farmer in my state and our businesses,' Hochul said. 'That is obviously emanating from Washington.'
As businesses and families brace for further impacts, Hochul said she is working on policies to mitigate some of the economic damage. 'Elections have consequences. This is one of the dire consequences of the election this past November,' she said. 'All I can do is try to fortify my state against the impacts.' Legislative Gazette photo by Jamie Case
Hochul's administration set up a line of communication for farmers to easily report the effects of these tariffs on their products, in real time, in their local markets.
The Empire State Development agency has created an email — TariffImpact@esd.ny.gov — dedicated to receiving stories, anecdotes and data about the ways Trump's tariffs are impacting New York farmers, food sales and other aspects of the agricultural industry.
'I want to know the impacts of tariffs on our farmers and people across the state,' Hochul said. 'Because I have to be able to quantify this and use this to build the argument when I'm speaking to our legislators, our Republican members of Congress who are in the majority.'
'I want to have the stories, the data, and be able to talk about the impact that these tariffs have had on the state of New York… This is the last thing our agricultural community needs — or our entire state needed — and this is now the reality we're having to deal with.'
With the economic strain expected to worsen, New York farmers say they are left with difficult decisions about the future.
'We were promised affordability,' Hochul said. 'Instead, prices are skyrocketing, and our small businesses are paying the price.'

title: Remembering Edward Griffith: 'The Most Decent Man in the Legislature'
author: JOHN J. HALLORAN
description: The Honorable Edward Griffith of Brooklyn, N.Y. passed on October 26, 2023, at 92 years of age, and it is important to recall and celebrate his life and legacy, as well as his enduring contributions…
content:
Photo courtesy of the New York State Assembly, circa 1980
From left, Assemblyman Edward Griffith, U.S. Senator Daniel Patrick Moynihan, and John Halloran. The Honorable Edward Griffith of Brooklyn, N.Y. passed on October 26, 2023, at 92 years of age, and it is important to recall and celebrate his life and legacy, as well as his enduring contributions to the law of New York.
From 1973 through 2000, Mr. Griffith represented the 40th Assembly District, which covered a portion of East New York, Brownsville, and East Flatbush, in Brooklyn, Kings County. He received his B.A. in education from the Canal Zone College in Panama, and a B.A. in Political Science from Queens College. Before his election to the Assembly, Mr. Griffith had a background in banking, served with the United Nations International School Association, and was the first president of Community School Board, District 19. He also served in the United States Air Force, as missile technician, from 1955 to 1961.
Mr. Griffith made vast contributions to New York law. He was the only nonlawyer on the Assembly Judiciary Committee for many years. This was a testament to his good judgment and deep understanding of the needs of the community. One of the Judiciary Committee's intellectual leaders, Ralph Goldstein of Queens, warmly praised 'Eddie' as 'the most decent man in the Legislature.'
Mr. Goldstein's view was shared by his colleagues who, through Assembly leadership, named Mr. Griffith as the Chair of the Assembly Ethics & Guidance Committee. The Committee was constituted by an equal number of Republicans and Democrats. The Committee included the best and brightest lawyers in the Assembly such as Hon. Arthur J. Cooperman and Hon. J. Kemp Hannon. As Chair of the Committee, Mr. Griffith authored the Ethics Manual for Members and Employees of the New York State Assembly (1981). He published a paper entitled Incompatibility of Office: The New York Perspective (1982). He introduced ethics legislation and prepared confidential advisory opinions. Much of this work was completed with the assistance of his distinguished counsel, Edward Desmond, Esq. of Buffalo, N.Y. The Committee was highly professional, nonpartisan, and it conducted its business by consensus.
Ethics Manual for Members and Employees of the New York State Assembly (1981). He published a paper entitled Incompatibility of Office: The New York Perspective (1982). He introduced ethics legislation and prepared confidential advisory opinions. Much of this work was completed with the assistance of his distinguished counsel, Edward Desmond, Esq. of Buffalo, N.Y. The Committee was highly professional, nonpartisan, and it conducted its business by consensus. Mr. Griffith was steadfastly committed to the people of his 40th Assembly District and he enjoyed a close working relationship with all community leaders.
In 1981, one of those leaders, Bishop Francis J. Mugavero of the Diocese of Brooklyn, reached out to Mr. Griffith to explain a crisis facing children attending nonpublic schools in New York state. Near the close of the legislative session, the State Education Department announced an alarming decision to terminate what was called 'suitable transportation' for children with 'handicapping conditions' to and from 'nonpublic schools.' Working late into the night, Mr. Griffith spearheaded emergency legislation to preserve the transportation services. Governor Hugh L. Carey issued a message of necessity to enable an immediate vote on the bill. The governor signed the bill into law as Chapter 996 of the Laws of 1981, which continues to protect our most vulnerable citizenry today.
Mr. Griffith was also a proponent of court reform. For example, the federal and state courts owe a continuing debt of gratitude to Mr. Griffith for his leadership in amending the State Constitution to give the New York Court of Appeals the power and discretion to answer certified questions of New York law from certain other courts, such as the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit. The procedure is called interjurisdictional certification and it serves important jurisprudential interests.
Mr. Griffith's leadership was commended by Chief Judge Judith S. Kaye and Kenneth I. Weissman ( Interactive Judicial Federalism: Certified Questions in New York , 69 Fordham L. Rev. 373, 387-393 (2000)) and Chief Judge Sol Wachtler ( Federalism is Alive and Well and Living in New York , 75 Alb. L. Rev. 659, 662 (2011)). 'Thirty years have passed since the certification procedure was adopted, and its results have met with enthusiastic approval.' Advisory Group to the New York State and Federal Judicial Council, at Forward (March 2016).
Interactive Judicial Federalism: Certified Questions in New York , 69 Fordham L. Rev. 373, 387-393 (2000)) and Chief Judge Sol Wachtler ( Federalism is Alive and Well and Living in New York , 75 Alb. L. Rev. 659, 662 (2011)). 'Thirty years have passed since the certification procedure was adopted, and its results have met with enthusiastic approval.' Advisory Group to the New York State and Federal Judicial Council, at Forward (March 2016). Mr. Griffith possessed genuine empathy and kindness. He was moved by the tragic death of boxer Willie Classen of the Bronx, who died from brain injuries after a brutal contest at Madison Square Garden's Felt Forum. For most of the 20th century, boxing in New York had been regulated by the so-called Walker Law, named after its sponsor, then-Senator James J. ('Jimmy') Walker. Mr. Griffith believed that the archaic law needed reform and that the risk of tragedies in the ring could be mitigated with common-sense regulation, such as requiring ambulances at matches and paramedical training for personnel. To that end, Mr. Griffith introduced boxing reform legislation to wide acclaim (George Vecsey, Safety in the Ring , New York Times, Page 21, Feb. 14, 1981).
