title: Hochul, James Preparing for Potential Legal Threats From Second Trump Administration
author: JANANI HARIRAM
description: Hours after Donald Trump declared victory for his second term in the White House, Gov. Kathy Hochul and State Attorney General Letitia James said they are preparing for potential legal threats to New…
content:
Photo by Susan Watts, courtesy of the Governor's Office
November 6, 2024 — Manhattan, NY — Governor Kathy Hochul and Attorney General Letitia James deliver remarks on the 2024 election. They announced a strengthened partnership, including new dedicated staff, to address potential federal legal threats to reproductive freedom, gun safety laws and other key issues.
Hours after Donald Trump declared victory for his second term in the White House, Gov. Kathy Hochul and State Attorney General Letitia James said they are preparing for potential legal threats to New York's abortion laws, gun laws, immigration policies, environmental protections and other civil rights.
While both Hochul and James congratulated Trump on his victory, they made it clear they do not support his administration or his values. Hochul said, 'I want to reassure all New Yorkers. I know for many of you this is not the electoral result you hoped for. I will tell you this, we have weathered worse storms.'
The governor went on to state, 'New York will remain a bastion for freedom' and spoke about a new Empire State Freedom Initiative — with a new dedicated staff and more frequent collaboration between the governor's and attorney general's office — intended to protect those who she said are most vulnerable to threats from the Trump administration.
'Our team will do whatever we have to do to identify any possible threats to these rights that we hold dear in the state of New York and protect New Yorkers,' Hochul said. 'This will include legislation, rulemaking, appropriations, and partnerships with our congressional delegation and including the Biden administration at this time.'
Hochul spoke about the infrastructure and economic development programs New York needs in order to create more local jobs and support the economy. She said, 'I will work with him [Trump] or anybody else regardless of party on these initiatives that will help New Yotkers.'
James took the podium after Hochul and said, 'If it is possible we will work with [Trump's] administration, but we will not compromise our integrity or values.' She added that while this result was unexpected, her team and those across the country have been studying the Republican playbook and planning for their responses.
She said, 'Despite what has happened on the national stage, we will continue to stand tall in the face of injustice' and urged New Yorkers not to be fearful but rather steadfast.

title: Congestion Pricing Plan Will Fund Clean-Air Programs in Low-Income Neighborhoods
author: JANANI HARIRAM
description: Part of Gov. Kathy Hochul's congestion pricing plan includes remedies for air pollution in and around low-income communities. Hochul's newly unveiled congestion pricing plan reduces the cost of the…
content:
Photo by Don Pollard, courtesy of the Governor's Office
November 14, 2024 — New York, NY — Governor Hochul announces a plan to begin implementing congestion pricing in New York City by early January. Front page photo by Susan Watts, Office of the Governor
Part of Gov. Kathy Hochul's congestion pricing plan includes remedies for air pollution in and around low-income communities.
Hochul's newly unveiled congestion pricing plan reduces the cost of the toll to enter the Central Business District of Manhattan from $15 to $9 for passenger cars. The new tolls will help fund $15 billion to support the MTA's current capital improvement plans and pay for programs to reduce air pollution in low-income neighborhoods.
'As I said from the start, a $15 toll was just too high in this economic climate,' Hochul said. 'That's why our plan cuts the daytime toll to $9 for cars. By getting congestion pricing underway and fully supporting the MTA capital plan, we'll unclog our streets, reduce pollution and deliver better public transit for millions of New Yorkers.'
The administration expects to achieve congestion reduction and air quality benefits, including a 5 percent reduction in vehicle miles traveled and a 10 percent reduction in the number of vehicles driving below 60th Street.
Under the proposed fee structure, motorcycles will be charged $4.50; small trucks and non-commuter buses, $14.40; and large trucks and sightseeing buses will pay $21.60. The plan goes into effect January 5, 2025.
MTA Chair and CEO Janno Lieber said, 'New Yorkers deserve cleaner air, safer streets and ambulances that can get to them without gridlock, and the governor is stepping up for them and for riders who need trains and buses to get them where they have to go.'
Hochul's plan includes directing some of the revenue from the new tolls to improve air quality in low-income areas. She plans to spend $20 million to establish an asthma center and case management program in the Bronx, as well as $15 million to replace diesel-powered Transport Refrigeration Units at Hunts Point Produce Market in the Bronx.
'We'll begin to drive down gridlock and the emissions as intended, and we'll deliver major environmental improvements for places like the Bronx,' Hochul said. 'So that lower income communities will not only benefit from improved public transit service, but also cleaner air.'
Additionally, $10 million is going to be used to install air filtration units in schools near highways, with another $10 million being funded into installing roadside vegetation. Another $20 million is going to be used to expand the New York City Clean Trucks Program, a rebate program to help replace diesel trucks with either electric, hybrid or alternative-fuel trucks operating in the nine-county metropolitan area.
'The governor's announcement assures that much-needed pollution-reduction funding will be flowing into environmental justice projects in the South Bronx,' said Eric Goldstein, the New York City environment director of the Natural Resources Defense Council.
Further proposals to reduce traffic congestion and pollution will be included with Hochul's Executive Budget proposal in January.
These include the expansion of the MTA-NYC Automated Camera Enforcement program to permit enforcement of 'blocking the box' violations at street intersections, authorization for the use of weigh-in-motion technology to help keep overweight vehicles off city streets, and permitting the city to impose a surcharge for street permits on construction projects that block traffic lanes.
These policies will prevent gridlock, keep traffic moving smoothly, and make efficient use of curb space.
Hochul's congestion pricing plan has support from groups such as the League of Conservation Voters and Environmental Advocates of New York.

title: Executive Budget Provides Relief For Middle Class, But Questions About Federal Assistance Remain
author: KYLE BREDBERG
description: Gov. Kathy Hochul's $252 billion Executive Budget addresses concerns over affordability and public safety without increasing taxes. Potential challenges from the federal government, however, are…
content:
Photo by Mike Groll, courtesy of the Governor's Office
January 21, 2025 — Albany, NY — Governor Kathy Hochul presents the Fiscal Year 2026 Executive Budget in the Red Room at the State Capitol.
Gov. Kathy Hochul's $252 billion Executive Budget addresses concerns over affordability and public safety without increasing taxes. Potential challenges from the federal government, however, are causing concern about the future of some programs.
The governor outlined the state's proposed spending for the upcoming year in her budget address on Jan. 21.
Her budget builds on the plans outlined in her 2025 State of the State address , including more than $5 billion in funding for proposals tackling affordability. This encompasses funding for her middle-class tax cut, inflation refund checks, free breakfast and lunch in public schools, and the expansion of the child tax credit.
'The impact of these policies will be simple — New Yorkers will have more money in their pockets and less worry in their lives,' Hochul wrote in her budget briefing book for fiscal year 2026.
The governor also furthered her support for expanding childcare. The state will invest $37.4 billion in school aid in 2026, the highest level of state aid in history. Additionally, $3 billion will go towards childcare and education initiatives. This includes $13 million to transition to distraction free classrooms, $110 million to build or renovate childcare centers, and $1.3 billion in new funding for SUNY and CUNY schools.
Public safety also received investment. The budget commits $370 million to gun violence prevention programs and $290 million to improve the effectiveness of the criminal justice system. A new allocation of $77 million was dedicated to pay for a six-month deployment of NYPD officers on every New York City subway train between 9 p.m. and 5 a.m., among other initiatives.
'Because when it comes to protecting every single New Yorker, I'll use every tool at our disposal,' Hochul said.
The proposed budget is the largest in New York history, $19 billion greater than the 2025-2026 Executive Budget.
According to Budget Director Blake Washington, this increase can largely be attributed to increases in Medicaid and the aforementioned school aid, which accounted for nearly 60 percent of the increase in operating expenses. Photo by Mike Groll, courtesy of the Governor's Office
Budget Director Blake Washington holds a Fiscal Year 2026 Executive Budget technical briefing in the Blue Room at the State Capitol.
According to the budget book, 'the state offers some of the most comprehensive and extensive Medicaid benefits in the nation,' and covers 7 million people. That coverage is projected to cost $35.4 billion, an increase of 14 percent from last year.
The budget also dedicates substantial funds to housing and the environment. Housing development programs will receive more than $2 billion, and the budget proposed the largest climate investment in New York history, dedicating over $1 billion towards new climate initiatives. 'These are all important priorities that the legislature also shares,' Hochul said.
Additional proposed investments, such as initiatives to improve the state's economic growth, transportation and health care also aligned with the governor's State of the State address. More detail on the budget proposal can be found in the budget briefing book.
In her address, Hochul also shared the growth of the state's rainy-day reserve, a fund of unallocated money that helps the state through uncertain financial circumstances. The fund has increased from 4 percent of the state's Operating Budget to nearly 15 percent during the governor's tenure, and is currently at a historic $21.1 billion, according to Hochul.
'We are in a good, strong, fiscal position,' Washington said.
Republican lawmakers disagree. 'A $252 billion budget disregards the fiscal responsibility required to ensure New York becomes truly affordable in the long run,' said Assembly Minority Leader Will Barclay in a press release. 'We can't spend our way into affordability and will never reduce the cost of living by forcing taxpayers to pay more, year after year.'
Barclay also stated concerns over how much the budget could grow. 'The most alarming part of the governor's $252 billion spending plan is that this is almost certainly the floor,' he said.
The previous year's Enacted Budget of $237 billion was $4 billion greater than that year's Executive Budget, and was then increased to $243 billion in the New York Mid-Year report.
'The numbers are solid. This is a balanced budget, there's no income tax increases, and we have record reserves,' Hochul said. 'If those three things were not true, it would be a different dynamic.' Photo by Mike Groll, courtesy of the Governor's Office
Legislative leaders listen to Gov. Kathy Hochul present her 2026 Executive Budget in the Capitol on January 21, 2025.
While Republican lawmakers cited concerns over how much was in the budget, a few notable proposals were absent from it.
First, the budget neglected to mention how the state intends to deal with President Donald Trump's public promise to end congestion pricing in New York City, something that Hochul states would result in '$15 billion of lost investment.'
Additionally, no plan to fill the $33 billion revenue gap in the 2025-2029 MTA capital plan was provided. The current proposed plan was previously voted down in Dec. 2024, as the Legislature could not identify a source of revenue for $33 billion of the $68 billion project.
'We will need to adopt a capital plan working in concert with the Legislature and MTA and that's something that will warrant further discussion in the upcoming months,' Washington said.
The new federal administration may also present other fiscal challenges.
According to the budget briefing book 'possible reductions in federal assistance that support vital New York programs, including health care delivery, social services, and public safety, could negatively impact the state and New Yorkers who depend on these programs.'
Responding to concerns over how the state will handle potential cuts in federal assistance, Hochul shifted the responsibility to New York state representatives in Congress, prompting them to pass a federal budget that aligns with the governor's goals. 'I'm putting responsibility where it belongs,' Hochul said.
Hochul also said if cuts to federal aid do happen, she would not commit to using the state's rainy-day reserves to support those programs.
'Elections have consequences,' Hochul said. 'I cannot stand here and say the state of New York is going to backfill all the federal dollars, no state governor can do that, and I'm not prepared to say that. It will be challenging.'

title: Gov. Hochul Meeting With Top Democrats About "The Path Forward" For New York City
author: JAMIE CASE
description: A controversial agreement between Mayor Eric Adams and President Donald Trump over the removal of immigrants in New York City has reignited discussions about Adams' potential removal from office…
content:
Photo by Susan Watts, courtesy of the Governor's Office
December 5, 2024 — New York, N.Y. — Governor Kathy Hochul and Mayor Eric Adams deliver remarks at a housing reform rally at City Hall. Hochul is facing pressure from some Democrats to remove Mayor Adams from office after federal corruption charges were dropped against the mayor in return for his cooperation with Trump Administration officials on immigration enforcement in New York.
A controversial agreement between Mayor Eric Adams and President Donald Trump over the removal of immigrants in New York City has reignited discussions about Adams' potential removal from office through an unprecedented use of the governor's powers.
Adams allegedly agreed to provide support to the Trump Administration on immigration issues in the Big Apple in exchange for dropping criminal charges against him.
This deal has led to the resignation of former U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York Danielle Sassoon and at least four senior managers in the Justice Department's Public Integrity Division.
According to the watchdog group Reinvent Albany, these resignations occurred as a result of the DOJ's decision to drop corruption charges against Adams, which included bribery and campaign finance violations. Adams has denied the allegations, and his trial is scheduled for April.
Reinvent Albany condemned the agreement, stating, 'This deal is a fundamental threat to the rule of law and the right of New York City voters to have a mayor who can act independently and in their best interest — rather than obeying President Trump's wishes or risk going to jail.'
The group was clear on its stance regarding Adams' removal.
'The governor has a responsibility to the people of New York City to restore the rule of law and democratic governance and must remove Mayor Adams from office immediately.'
Under the City Charter and New York State Constitution , the governor has the authority to remove the mayor. Gov. Kathy Hochul would have to present Adams with the charges and allow him to defend himself. If she moves forward, Adams would be suspended for up to 30 days while making his case. Hochul could then choose to reinstate him or permanently remove him from office.
This is not the first time Gov. Hochul has faced this decision. After Adams' indictment was unsealed last September, calls for his removal also surfaced.
Late last week, she addressed the situation on MSNBC's The Rachel Maddow Show.
'The allegations are extremely concerning and serious, but I cannot, as the governor of this state, have a knee-jerk, politically motivated reaction like a lot of other people are saying right now,' Hochul said. 'I have to do what's smart, what's right, and I'm consulting with other leaders in government at this time.'
Hochul released a statement Monday night saying she would meet with key Democratic leaders to discuss 'the path forward.'
'I recognize the immense responsibility I hold as governor and the constitutional powers granted to this office,' Gov. Hochul said on Monday. 'In the 235 years of New York state history, these powers have never been utilized to remove a duly-elected mayor; overturning the will of the voters is a serious step that should not be taken lightly.
'That said, the alleged conduct at City Hall that has been reported over the past two weeks is troubling and cannot be ignored. I have asked key leaders to meet me at my Manhattan office [on Tuesday] for a conversation about the path forward, with the goal of ensuring stability for the city of New York,' Hochul continued.
'Let me be clear: my most urgent concern is the well-being of my 8.3 million constituents who live in New York City. I will be monitoring this situation extraordinarily closely to ensure that New Yorkers are not being shortchanged by the current crisis in city government.'

title: Citizen Action Condemns Immigration Raids in Ithaca, New York City
author: LILLY SABELLA
description: President Donald Trump has wasted no time delivering on the promise of mass deportations he made while on the campaign trail. One month into his second presidency, New York state is no exception to…
content:
Photo Courtesy of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement
President Donald Trump has wasted no time delivering on the promise of mass deportations he made while on the campaign trail.
One month into his second presidency, New York state is no exception to the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids reported throughout the nation. Officers have arrested people believed to be living in the country illegally in Ithaca and New York City, two well-known sanctuary communities in New York.
According to reporting by The City , authorities have arrested over 100 people in New York City. The federal immigration agency had been uploading daily statistics on its total number of arrests made and people detained to social media , but these updates appeared to have stopped, with the last update on Feb. 1.
The grassroots activist group Citizen Action of New York condemned the raids. 'These raids are not about public safety — they are about tearing families apart, criminalizing Black and Brown communities, and instilling fear in our neighbors. This is government-sanctioned racial profiling, and we will not stand by in silence,' Citizen Action of New York said in a statement.
The city of Ithaca responded to the raids by reinforcing a policy prohibiting city officials and police from helping ICE enforce federal immigration policy. Ithaca's Common Council reaffirmed the 1985 sanctuary city resolution in a unanimous vote made on Feb. 5.
'We will not be silent while families are torn apart,' Citizen Action said in its statement. 'We will not be silent while our neighbors live in fear. From Ithaca to Buffalo, to Long Island, we will fight for a New York that stands for justice, dignity, and human rights for all.'
Lilly Sabella is a fourth-year student from Queens, New York. She moved upstate to New Paltz to pursue her undergraduate English degree with a minor in political science. While at SUNY New Paltz, she has served as News Editor and Features Editor for The Oracle, as Nonfiction Editor for Columbia University's literary magazine, Exchange, and has been published in Rewire News Group. You can read more of her writing on her blog lillysabella.substack.com.

title: Delgado Announces Split from Hochul, Preps For His Own Future Campaign
author: LILLY SABELLA
description: Lt. Gov. Antonio Delgado is breaking from Gov. Kathy Hochul in a decision not to be her running mate for the 2026 gubernatorial election. His announcement comes after public indications of a schism…
content:
Legislative Gazette file photo
Lt. Gov. Antonio Delgado is breaking from Gov. Kathy Hochul in a decision not to be her running mate for the 2026 gubernatorial election. His announcement comes after public indications of a schism between Delgado and the governor.
Hochul selected the former congressman to serve alongside her following Andrew Cuomo's resignation. Delgado's choice to step down from another term may signal plans to make his own bid for the governor's office.
On February 25, Delgado registered with the New York State Board of Elections for an undeclared office, opening the door for a future campaign in New York state.
'All options are on the table, and I will be exploring them,' he said in the statement announcing his decision.
Two weeks ago, Delgado publicly disagreed with Hochul when he urged Mayor Eric Adams to step down from his post. Hochul, who has since refused to remove Adams, had emphasized exercising caution instead of rushing to a decision involving the embittered New York mayor's political future. Disagreements between the governor and her second-in-command are seldom a public affair, making Delgado's dissent a clear mark of their fractured relationship.
'When I first made the decision to run for office after the 2016 presidential election, I did so because I believed we needed more leaders in government willing to hold themselves accountable to the people — and only the people,' Delgado said on Monday. 'I believe New Yorkers deserve this kind of leadership now more than ever.'
A response from the Governor's Office, attributed to Communications Director Anthony Hogrebe, confirmed their soured relationship.
'Antonio Delgado finally said out loud what has been obvious for quite some time: he is simply not interested in doing the job of the lieutenant governor of the state of New York,' Hogrebe's statement said.
In a clear indication of bad blood, the statement included that Hochul's administration will be reallocating responsibilities away from Delgado's office to ensure they 'are no longer neglected' and that Hochul was already considering a different running mate before Delgado's announcement.
'Governor Hochul had already begun taking steps to identify a new running mate for 2026,' Hogrebe said. 'Governor Hochul wishes him the best in his future endeavors.'
The Eric Adams debacle is not the first time Delgado and Hochul have appeared out of sync. While Hochul steadfastly supported Joe Biden for president last year, Delgado joined the wave of Democrats putting pressure on the former president to exit the race.
Delgado, a Schenectady native, is a former Division 1 athlete at Colgate University, a Rhodes scholar and Harvard Law School graduate.
Before joining up with Hochul, Delgado served three and a half years in Congress, winning a Hudson Valley swing district after a race that made national headlines when incumbent John Faso criticized Delgado for his brief endeavor as a rapper.
Despite these attacks, he became the first Black or Latino representative in upstate New York.
Delgado says he intends to finish his full term as lieutenant governor, through the end of 2026.
'I remain deeply committed to finishing my full term, as I was independently elected to do by the people of New York,' he said.
